abstract: Statistical contracts reward experimenters according to the evidence produced by a costly study, so the reward rule influences both who participates and what they report. Principal--agent testing theory explains how to prevent ineffective proposals from being profitable. We ask when such contracts can also elicit honest parameter reports if the decision concerns a mean effect but the variance or distributional shape is unknown. Under risk neutrality and a fixed participation cost, we construct menus of e-values --- nonnegative normalized rewards with expected value at most one under every null --- such that (i) agents who know they are null have no incentive to participate, (ii) every alternative type earns positive expected profit and is thus incentivized to participate, (iii) truthful reporting uniquely maximizes expected their reward, (iv) and each contract is admissible: its payouts cannot be pointwise improved while retaining null validity. For Gaussian observations, we treat separately agents who know both mean and variance and agents who know only their mean; in the latter case, truthfulness holds at every variance without requiring a nuisance prior. Multi-sample extensions preserve these incentives and can reward accumulating evidence. Beyond Gaussian models, we show that two independent nonnegative observations suffice to elicit any finite mean above a positive null threshold, without any further distributional knowledge, but one observation cannot combine strict mean elicitation with individual admissibility on this class. Finally, we distinguish the existence of useful tests from the identification needed for truthful contracts. Boundedness is not required, and finitely many null constraints do not by themselves guarantee admissible elicitation.

title: Deterministic Implementation of Mean-Preserving Contractions
abstract: We study whether randomization is needed to generate a prescribed distribution of posterior means for a one-dimensional state. Drawing on backward Monge martingale transport, we show that every mean-preserving contraction of an atomless prior with finite first moment admits a deterministic implementation. Consequently, restricting attention to deterministic signals leaves the designer's value unchanged whenever objectives and constraints depend only on the posterior-mean distribution. We decompose implementation into independent problems on non-separating intervals and describe a constructive procedure based on barcode transport. We also characterize when lower or upper contour sets can take a nested-interval form, and provide applications to monopolistic pricing with buyer-optimal learning and robust persuasion with ambiguous receiver preferences.

title: Quantifying Blinking Suppression and Probing Its Mechanism in PPD-Treated Single Quantum Dots
abstract: Colloidal semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are highly promising materials for various applications, yet photoluminescence intermittency (blinking) remains a key obstacle to their practical use. While recent advances have enabled partial or complete suppression of this effect, both the degree of suppression and the mechanism by which it occurs are often difficult to establish. In the present work we analyse the blinking suppression of single CdSe/ZnS QDs after treatment with p-phenylenediamine (PPD), recently discovered by Yang et al. We revisit the blinking mechanism in this system and show that it is governed predominantly by the trapping mechanism, rather than by Auger ionization as previously proposed. For data analysis we apply a threshold-free two-dimensional criterion recently proposed by Podshivaylov and Frantsuzov. The criterion is based on the relative quantum yield estimator $\langle \hat{Q} \rangle^{(s)}$ and the decay-rate fluctuation parameter $\hatξ$. We found that PPD treatment significantly increases the relative quantum yield and leads to only a modest increase in $\hatξ$, indicating that the dominant effect of PPD is to shift the distribution of the non-radiative recombination rate toward lower values, rather than to eliminate its fluctuations. We further suggest a number of possible mechanisms of PPD-induced suppression and propose critical experiments for their verification.

title: On the Turán number for the Cartesian product of an odd cycle and a tree
abstract: Let $T$ be a fixed tree on at least two vertices. We determine the Turán number and all extremal graphs for the Cartesian product of an odd cycle $C_{2m+1}$ and $T$, for every fixed integer $m\ge1$ and all sufficiently large $n$, in terms of its decomposition family. Every extremal graph is the join of an independent set and an extremal graph for that family. The proof combines the Erdős--Sós theorem with weak stability and progressive induction.

title: Semipositivity and complete subvarieties of projectivised strata of holomorphic differentials
abstract: We show that if the projectivised stratum $\mathbb{P}{H}_g(μ)$ associated to a partition $μ=(m_1,\ldots,m_n)$ of $2g-2$ contains a complete curve, then \[ \sum_{i=1}^n\frac{m_i(m_i+2)}{m_i+1}>12. \] The weak inequality follows from semipositivity applied to a quotient of the Hodge bundle, while equality is excluded using the second Fujita decomposition and the geometry of fibred surfaces with maximal unitary rank. Consequently, no projectivised holomorphic stratum in genus $g\leq5$ contains a positive-dimensional complete subvariety. In genus $g=6$ the same conclusion holds for signatures \[ (10),\ (9,1),\ (8,2),\ (8,1,1),\ (7,3),\ (6,4),\ (5,5). \]

title: Shielding design and construction for the XINGZHI cold neutron triple-axis spectrometer: integrating velocity selector, S-bender polarizer, and neutron guide
abstract: The optimized design and construction of shielding for the velocity selector, S-bender polarizer, and neutron guide in the XINGZHI cold neutron triple-axis spectrometer have been successfully completed. The challenge of limited space available for XINGZHI has been met by a compact shielding structure, developed through Monte Carlo simulations and realized by purpose-built mechanical design, thus leaving more floor space for the spectrometer. An innovative lead-antimony alloy ensures rigidity for self-support, while optimized tolerances for gaps between mating blocks meet safety, machinability, and mounting requirements. Additionally, a long-distance alignment method has been implemented, facilitating the alternating installation of the neutron guide and shielding system. After six years of operation, this structure has been verified to meet radiation safety standards while maximizing available space, marking a significant advancement in neutron instrumentation in China and offering valuable methodologies for future development.

title: PsyInterviewee: Informational Invariance and Relational Adaptivity in Mental Health Interview Simulation
abstract: LLM-based simulated interviewees support interviewer training and the evaluation of mental health interviewing systems. Existing studies have primarily focused on improving human-likeness through richer patient profiles and behavioral modeling. However, human-likeness alone does not establish their reliability. Reliable simulation requires preserving profile-grounded clinical facts (informational invariance) while adapting disclosure and interaction behavior to the interview (relational adaptivity). To this end, we introduce PsyInterviewee, which separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel and verifies generated clinical claims against the profile. Specifically, asymmetric write permissions allow dialogue context to update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts; these states guide what profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. In an automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee achieves higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations suggest that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.

title: SAT-ACT: Learning CDCL Branching from Outcome-Derived Action Preferences
abstract: Learning-based approaches have increasingly been explored for SAT solving, with particular attention to improving branching decisions in conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) solvers. These approaches derive branching guidance either from static structural properties of SAT formulas or from dynamic signals obtained through solver feedback and execution traces. However, these forms of supervision provide limited evidence about state-dependent branching effects, while different outcome measures may favor different branching choices. To address these limitations, we propose SAT-ACT, an outcome-derived learning framework for CDCL branching. We design three complementary outcome comparison criteria to extract action preferences from independent branching action rollouts initiated at the same solver state. The criteria identify preferences supported by the outcomes and leave comparisons unresolved when the evidence is insufficient or conflicting, instead of forcing an ordering using a predefined scalar metric. A state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from the extracted preferences and uses them to guide CDCL search directly without online action rollouts. We further introduce non-dominated heuristic action supervision, which retains the solver-selected action as a training target only when it remains non-dominated under these preferences. Solver-level experiments show that SAT-ACT consistently reduces CDCL search costs on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on the SAT Competition benchmarks.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

title: From Transcription to Reformulation: Defining and Benchmarking Grounded Generative Speech Recognition
abstract: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.

title: Is XTE J1814-338 a dark matter-admixed neutron star?
abstract: We explore the possibility that the ultracompact object XTE J1814-338 is a dark matter-admixed neutron star (DNS) based on a general-relativistic two-fluid approach, in which one fluid describes ordinary nuclear matter and the other dark matter. The equations of state of nuclear matter and dark matter are described by the Brueckner-Hartree-Fock (BHF) theory with realistic three-body forces and a generic bosonic self-interacting dark matter model, respectively. Based on the observational data, we determine the parameter space for XTE J1814-338 as a DNS, and find that only a halo stellar configuration with a high dark matter fraction is allowed. Furthermore, we predict other observable properties of XTE J1814-338 and provide robust lower bounds for these quantities.

title: The Double Diagonal Estimator: Reducing Bias in Two-Sided Marketplace Experiments
abstract: Interference between participants in two-sided marketplace experiments can severely bias conventional A/B tests. While two-sided randomization (TSR), which randomizes both supply and demand, enables estimators that mitigate this bias, existing analyses offer limited guidance on which estimator to prefer for the balanced market conditions common in practice, as they largely focus on extreme supply- or demand-constrained regimes. We introduce the Double Diagonal (DD) estimator, a novel method for interference-robust treatment effect estimation. The DD estimator contrasts the outcomes of treated-treated and control-control pairs and uses the off-diagonal interactions (treated-control and control-treated) to correct for interference-induced bias. We provide the first theoretical comparison between the DD and the standard naive TSR (TSRN) estimator under a simplifying mean-field market model, proving two key results: (i) DD's bias is strictly smaller than the standard estimator's below a critical threshold of the outside-option parameter; in particular, DD's bias is smaller whenever the outside option is at most twice as attractive as platform options; and (ii) the two estimators exhibit biases in opposite directions, with DD underestimating and the standard estimator overestimating the true effect, respectively. Extensive numerical experiments in realistic market settings--spanning heterogeneous treatment effects, supply-demand imbalances, and varied market structures--corroborate our theoretical findings. Across a wide range of configurations, the DD estimator demonstrates the lowest bias, establishing it as a robust and often superior choice for reliable experimentation in two-sided marketplaces.

title: Assortativity and the Distribution of Spectral Gaps in Directed Networks
abstract: This paper studies how the distribution of spectral gaps of a weighted directed network varies with its assortativity. We prove that the sum of the distances of each of the eigenvalues from the Perron root along the real axis, which we call the `spectral depth', decreases as the network is rewired to be less assortative. The result is conditional on the network's Perron vectors ordering the rewired vertices in the same way as their strengths do. We also develop a method to determine whether a particular spectral gap contracts or expands under a rewiring that changes the network's assortativity. It turns out that the direction of any one gap depends on far more than the network's assortativity. In computational experiments on heavy-tailed networks, disassortative rewiring lowers the spectral depth by about two fifths, contracts most strongly the gaps in the middle of the spectrum, and collapses a growing part of the spectrum to zero. The experiments also show that a sequence of disassortative rewirings tends to narrow the first spectral gap, while a sequence of assortative rewirings widens it.

title: Self-Improvement with Auxiliary Rewards: Learning from Verified Traces and Evaluating Transfer
abstract: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.

title: Rigidity in sharp eigenvalue estimates for differential forms
abstract: For $1\leq p\leq n/2$, we derive sharp eigenvalue estimates for the Hodge Laplacian on differential $p$-forms under the curvature condition introduced by Petersen and Wink, and study their equality cases. Equality recovers the stronger curvature operator lower bound and, in the closed case, leaves only round or Sasakian metrics on the universal cover. For manifolds with boundary, weak $p$-convexity of the boundary makes the unit hemisphere the only equality case for the absolute boundary problem.

title: Vector Valued Katok-Sarnak Formulas
abstract: We introduce a version of the Katok-Sarnak formula linking twisted traces of scalar valued Maass cusp forms for $Γ_0(N)$ with $N$ square-free to Fourier coefficients of vector valued Maass cusp forms for the metaplectic group $\operatorname{Mp}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and the Weil representation associated to a lattice of signature $(2,1)$. We prove this by computing the Fourier coefficients of the vector valued Siegel and Millson theta lift of a scalar valued newform by two different methods and comparing the results.

title: Stochastic dynamics generation of directed percolation using a two-channel convolutional neural network
abstract: Neural networks provide a promising approach to learning and generating the stochastic dynamics of nonequilibrium systems. In this study, we propose a stochastic dynamics generative method based on a two-channel convolutional neural network, using the (1+1)-dimensional directed bond percolation model to investigate its ability to learn local stochastic transition rules and reproduce stochastic dynamics across different system sizes. The proposed method takes the current particle configuration and the control parameter as inputs, learns the conditional activation probabilities at the next time step through local convolutions, and generates stochastic temporal evolution through iterative Bernoulli sampling. The results show that the network-generated dynamics agree well with Monte Carlo simulations across different control parameters. Furthermore, applying the trained network to a substantially larger system with $L=10000$ yields an estimated critical probability of $p_c=0.643$ and an effective density decay exponent of $δ\approx0.1592$, close to the established theoretical values. These findings demonstrate that the proposed method can reproduce the stochastic dynamics of directed percolation and capture its macroscopic dynamical and statistical properties across different spatial sizes.

title: Toward Low-Burden Image-Based Dietary Assessment Through Human-AI Collaborative Correction
abstract: Image-based dietary assessment can automate initial food logging, but meal photographs often leave food identity, hidden ingredients, preparation, and portion uncertain, making correction a recurring part of use. We introduce Human-AI Collaborative Correction, which reframes correction as communicate intent $\rightarrow$ regenerate $\rightarrow$ verify: users express what should change through text, voice, or guided clarification, the AI regenerates the linked dietary record, and users verify the result. In a within-participant study with 30 participants, compared with conventional Manual Search-and-Edit Correction, collaborative correction was associated with lower workload (Raw TLX: 35.83 vs. 55.00; p < .001), 21.0% lower recorded usage time, 51.1% fewer recorded clicks, and more favorable user-experience ratings; 90.0% preferred it overall. An exploratory nutrient analysis also found lower energy MAE. These findings support intent-driven regeneration as a promising interaction pattern for reducing correction burden while preserving user verification and making image-based dietary tracking easier to sustain.

title: Subliminal Reinforcement Learning: traits travel through a judge's scores
abstract: Subliminal learning, the transfer of a model's trait through data with no semantic trace of it, has been shown for students trained on a teacher's text. Post-training relies on group relative policy optimization with a language-model judge, where the student learns only from its own outputs and one judge's scores. We show this suffices: a student writes invented syllables or numbers, a judge made to prefer one animal scores them, and the student's preference moves toward that animal relative to a run whose judge prefers another. Of 48 design cells, two fail the validity gate and 17 establish the trait at 5% false-discovery rate, numbers-only cells included; elsewhere, our account gives the reason. Removing only the reward difference between judges removes transfer. We establish the principle as a chain of four stages: the trait must show in the judge's scores, favour strings that move the student, accumulate and reach the answers. Judges with the same preference built from other data, or on another model, place it on other strings, and transfer is not detected. Carried unchanged to AI-safety dispositions, the chain holds: undesirable dispositions reach the student's answers, and stages measured before training anticipate where, helping to prevent part of this risk.

title: Scaled-Gradient Hard Thresholding Algorithms for Sparse Signal Recovery
abstract: Thresholding methods provide a simple iterative framework for sparse signal recovery by combining a search direction with a thresholding operation. Gradient-based search directions are computationally efficient because they require only first-order information for the error metric. We incorporate componentwise gradient scaling into this framework by preserving large-magnitude components and attenuating the remaining components of the gradient of error metric. Combining this strategy with hard thresholding yields scaled-gradient hard thresholding (SGHT) and its pursuit variant SGHTP. Under suitable restricted isometry conditions, we establish recovery error bounds for both methods that account for measurement noise and deviations from exact sparsity. Numerical experiments indicate that SGHTP achieves recovery performance comparable to established pursuit methods on the tested ECG signals.

title: rl_rob: A transparent, from-scratch Python library for teaching reinforcement learning from tabular methods to deep policy gradients
abstract: rl_rob is an open-source Python library for teaching reinforcement learning. It implements the arc of a modern course, from tabular temporal-difference learning through linear function approximation to deep value-based and policy-gradient methods, with every algorithm written from first principles so that its update rule is visible in a few lines of code. All agents share one interface, so learners can compare methods directly across stages and trace a deep reinforcement learning update from the temporal-difference error to the weight change. The library supports teaching and assessment in which students implement, modify and explain update rules, rather than only produce working code.

title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

title: Feature-preserving interface reconstruction using piecewise circles and cusps
abstract: We present a geometric interface reconstruction method for Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) simulations that captures both curved interfaces and sharp features using only volume fraction data. We represent interfaces with linear facets, circular arcs, and corner facets formed by two lines or arcs joined within a single cell. We first propagate local orientation constraints through a graph and merge cells to resolve ambiguities, treating topological consistency as a first-class constraint. An optional conservative refinement improves $C^0$ continuity while preserving local volume constraints. Users can independently enable circular facets, corner facets, cell merging, and continuity refinement to balance accuracy and computational cost. In its simplest configuration, our method provides a fast local line-fitting scheme competitive with state-of-the-art PLIC methods. On standard static benchmarks, the full configuration reconstructs identifiable lines, circles, and sufficiently resolved corners to numerical precision on coarse, perturbed Cartesian meshes. On varying-curvature interfaces, it achieves third-order convergence in facet-gap error and approximately first-order convergence in curvature error. These results demonstrate global volume conservation and accurate reconstruction of curved and corner features.

title: Pebbling Numbers and Generator Reinforcement of Cayley Graphs
abstract: We study inverse-closed generator additions of minimum size that make the optimal pebbling number of a finite Cayley graph at most three while preserving its specified regular action. A weighted vertex-cover formulation on inverse orbits yields an $O(|Γ|^2)$ algorithm for abelian groups in the explicit multiplication-table model. We derive formulas for central involutions and cubelike graphs, with an inverse-closure correction determined by square roots in the uncovered set. The exact thresholds are $2^{d-1}-d$ for hypercubes ($d\ge1$), and $3$ for standard Keller graphs when $d=2$ and $2^{d-1}$ when $d\ge3$. Every admissible augmentation of either family has ordinary pebbling number equal to its order.

title: Erase the Injected Region: Multimodal Prompt-Injection Defense with On-Policy Self-Distillation
abstract: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation. We propose ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method that constructs its reference by erasing the injected region in place. Modality-appropriate blank content replaces the injection while the surrounding media is preserved. A student reading attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts. Across image, audio, and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark while retaining task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio, ERASE reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy compared with ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level. Experiments show that ERASE reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio while staying close to the base model on the erased input. Out-of-domain accuracy also stays near the base level. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

title: SERIAL-7: Deriving, Realizing, and Preserving Machine-Verifiable Outputs Across Representations
abstract: Large language models increasingly generate structured outputs consumed by programs and downstream systems, where semantic correctness alone does not guarantee reliable execution. We introduce SERIAL-7, a Korean-English benchmark built around an executable verification framework for machine-verifiable generation across seven representations. Using 177 validated canonical artifacts, SERIAL-7 separates semantic derivation (Derive), constrained artifact generation (Realize), and cross-representation preservation (Preserve). Its 43 atomic representation constraints are paired with executable checks over format, structure, and task-specific semantics, enabling progressively stricter verification from representation compliance to full artifact validity. Across ten models, REALIZE-L3 HSR ranges from 42.0% to 93.9%, while Full Compliance exposes additional artifact-level failures beyond correct final answers and valid representations. These results show that reliable structured generation requires explicit, executable verification of how artifacts are realized and preserved across representations.

title: Product Pitt inequalities and signed Boas equivalences for general monotone functions
abstract: We prove product-weight Pitt inequalities for real or complex functions on $\mathbb R^d$ whose full mixed Vitali variation satisfies an exterior-tail general monotonicity condition. A two-parameter condition gives spatial weights with different powers near the coordinate hyperplanes and at infinity. For the classical parameters, a reverse estimate yields a Boas norm equivalence without sign, parity or separability assumptions. The equivalence holds for finite spatial norm and, for $L^1$ data, characterizes finiteness of either norm; the unrestricted nonintegrable converse remains open. We also prove an equivalence under primitive control, give explicit examples, and establish sharpness of the Fourier-side exponent range.

title: STAR-FER: Adaptive Selective Restoration for Edge-Based Low-Resolution Facial Expression Recognition
abstract: Variable interaction distances continuously degrade facial resolution in edge-based affective interaction, making low-resolution facial expression recognition (FER) difficult under limited computation. Full-face image or feature restoration incurs substantial overhead, whereas lightweight recognition pipelines may miss local cues that remain discriminative after degradation. We propose STAR-FER, a scale-and-task-adaptive selective restoration framework that balances recognition performance and resource constraints. A lightweight image-scale conditioned Gate jointly predicts a pixel-wise spatial ranking and a continuous restoration budget, then applies exact-support projection to obtain an input-dependent free-form mask. The mask-conditioned restorer retains complete facial context while concentrating sparse restoration and residual insertion on the selected support. Across seven degradation scales from x2 to x8 on the complete RAF-DB test set, STAR-FER achieves 80.92% mean accuracy and 71.64% Macro-F1, improving the low-resolution ResNet-18 baseline by 2.25 and 2.71 percentage points, respectively. It surpasses SR-FER by 1.04 accuracy points while requiring 8.84 GFLOPs, a 54.29% reduction, with 28.01% mean mask coverage, and maintains effective recognition at unseen non-integer scales. These results show that spatial-ranking and continuous-budget driven selective restoration reduces spatial modification and computation while maintaining low-resolution FER performance, offering an efficient path to resource-constrained affective interaction.

title: Optimality of the Petz-Fuchs Smoothed State
abstract: Quantum state smoothing is an estimation technique that uses past and future measurement information obtained from a continuous-in-time measurement record to reconstruct the state of an open quantum system. Recently, there has been a new approach to quantum state smoothing based on quantum retrodiction known as the Petz-Fuchs smoothed state. Here I prove that this Petz-Fuchs smoothed state majorizes all other smoothed states that only depend on the filtered state (the operator conditioned on the past measurement record) and the retrofiltered effect (the operator describing the future measurement record). To do this, I characterize the set of all possible smoothed states satisfying this condition.

title: A Model for Fast Mining Blockchains
abstract: We study a Markovian model for a blockchain mining process. In the limit where there is an infinite number of miners, the model satisfies a functional law of large numbers due to Barbour and Luczac (2008), leading to an infinite set of coupled ODEs characterising the blockchain heights. We show that the sequence of solutions to this system converges uniformly, to a limiting profile in an appropriate comoving frame. Utilising asymptotic arguments inspired by Brunet and Derrida (1997), we derive an explicit expression for the position of the travelling front, which exhibits a leading order logarithmic Bramson correction in time. For a finite number of miners, we further derive a correction to the travelling speed which is logarithmic in the number of miners. Finally, by application of a computation due to Ablowitz and Zeppetella (1979), we identify that, for a specific choice of the travelling speed, the Painlevé integrable, travelling wave solution of the Fisher-KPP equation with drift accurately matches our limiting profile. Our results are supported by numerical simulations.

title: Migrating a Legacy Scientific Application with an AI Coding Agent: NICAM from Fortran to Kokkos
abstract: Migrating from Fortran to C++/Kokkos broadens access to hardware accelerators through backends such as CUDA and HIP while offering greater flexibility in software design. However, legacy Fortran applications often have large codebases, making manual porting time-consuming and costly. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and AI coding agents have made large-scale code migration increasingly feasible. In this study, we ported NICAM (Nonhydrostatic ICosahedral Atmospheric Model), a legacy Fortran climate model accelerated with OpenACC, to C++/Kokkos with the assistance of Claude Code. The agent translated the code directly from Fortran to C++/Kokkos under human review. Approximately 140,000 lines of Fortran were analyzed and ported into 35,000 lines of C++/Kokkos, covering the dynamical core and seven physics packages. A 100-member ensemble comparison with the original Fortran model showed that the port is statistically consistent with the original. Performance was evaluated on Miyabi-G, an NVIDIA GH200 cluster, and Sirius, an AMD MI300A cluster. Compared with the Fortran/OpenACC baseline on GH200, the port achieved application speedups of $1.71\times$ on GH200 and $1.54\times$ on MI300A. The CUDA build achieved a GPU kernel-time speedup of $1.38\times$ on GH200. After normalization by peak memory bandwidth, the HIP build on MI300A achieved $0.96\times$ the kernel performance of the Fortran/OpenACC baseline.

title: GenDSR: Transferring Representations from Video Generation Models for Dynamic Spatial Reasoning
abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning is essential for connecting visual intelligence to thephysical world, yet remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), which must preserve scene state while tracking how spatial relations evolve over time. Meanwhile, video generation models (VGMs), trained to synthesize temporally coherent world dynamics, offer a rich source of spatiotemporal representations. We present GenDSR, a framework that transfers intermediate representations from VGM into VLM for dynamic spatial reasoning. Rather than treating a VGM feature as a monolithic prior, GenDSR constructs two complementary branches: a raw branch preserving holistic generative context and a delta branch emphasizing temporal variation. Task-conditioned tokenwise gates then fuse both signals and inject the result into the native visual representation. On DSR-Bench, GenDSR achieves 67.2%, surpassing the previous best result and establishing a new state of the art.

title: Dual-rate optical frequency comb based on a cylindrical microresonator with a nanoscale radius variation
abstract: We theoretically find that a cylindrical microresonator with nanoscale radius variation can be a source of coherent microcombs with two repetition rates, independently controlled by the device geometry. This phenomenon arises from the formation of two-dimensional axial-azimuthal dissipative Kerr solitons (2D DKS), which we discovered through numerical simulations of the nonlinearly coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations with realistic microresonator device parameters. We demonstrate that, despite the variation in the dispersion characteristics of azimuthal modes at different axial numbers, the spontaneous synchronization mechanism leads to a unified soliton repetition rate. We consider near-parabolic variations in the radius of a cylindrical resonator, compatible with the surface nanoscale axial photonics (SNAP) platform. In our example, we generate 2D DKS with an azimuthal rate of approximately 329 GHz and an axial rate of 6 GHz, which can be adjusted on demand by selecting the appropriate resonator geometry, thereby promising compact sources of frequency combs operating simultaneously across different frequency scales.

title: Only the immortal can (almost) flock while turning: Two-dimensional chiral immortal flocks, time crystals and non-universal sub-logarithmic roughness
abstract: We study two-dimensional chiral ``dry'' (non-momentum conserving) ``immortal'' (number conserving) ``flocks'' (polar ordered active fluids). Noise driven fluctuations about the noise-free ``time crystal'' state, in which the velocity rotates uniformly in time, obey coupled Kardar-Parisi-Zhang-like equations for the local velocity orientation and a conserved concentration field; the latter field stabilizes order. Orientational fluctuations grow only sub-logarithmically, and number fluctuations are suppressed (``hyperuniform''); both exhibit nonuniversal scaling exponents. There are three different universality classes of disordering transitions.

title: PyQLAS: A Quantum-Classical Hybrid Solver Library for Linear Systems
abstract: Quantum algorithms solve a linear system at a cost that grows only polylogarithmically in its dimension, but on present-day hardware that advantage is realised only if the quantum and the classical parts of a solve are apportioned deliberately. We present PyQLAS, a quantum--classical hybrid library for linear systems that exposes this apportionment as a design parameter rather than a fixed assumption. PyQLAS builds three nested solvers around a single variational core---a variational solver, an outer residual iteration, and a Krylov-subspace projection---so that the quantum subroutine can be held at a fixed circuit width while the classical host absorbs the growth of the problem. Around them, the library supplies preconditioning at two independent levels, dimension alignment, checkpointing, and device-budget control, and a solve written against the interface runs unchanged on an exact state-vector simulator, on a local sampler, and on a real superconducting processor. The library is validated on the IEEE 118-bus power flow, a standard test system in which the linear solver is embedded in a classical Newton iteration. There, the iteration converges to the specified tolerance and reproduces the classical reference solution to within $2.3\times10^{-8}$ p.u.\ in voltage magnitude and $3.4\times10^{-6}$ degrees in voltage angle.

title: Sparse descent subspace-Newton thresholding algorithm for sparse optimization problems
abstract: In this paper, we propose a sparse descent direction derived from the Newton direction within a low-dimensional subspace for sparse optimization problems. Building upon this direction and incorporating hard thresholding and orthogonal projection, we develop a novel algorithm termed the sparse descent subspace-Newton thresholding (SDSNT) algorithm. We further establish its global convergence under the restricted isometry property $δ_{3k}\leq \sqrt{3/20}$ of the measurement matrix. Numerical experiments on random sparse vector recovery and audio signal reconstruction reveal that SDSNT achieves comparable performance to several state-of-the-art algorithms. Notably, relative to most of them, it delivers superior recovery at high sparsity levels and improved efficiency at low sparsity levels.

title: MILES-Rec: Uncovering Implicit Intents from Mobility Behaviors for Cross-Domain POI Recommendation
abstract: Map applications bridge everyday mobility with local services, creating opportunities to recommend places by uncovering users' implicit intents. However, utility-driven map interactions provide only indirect and incomplete evidence of consumption demands, making it challenging to infer personalized service needs from observed behaviors. We propose MILES-Rec, a cross-domain POI recommendation framework that infers latent service intents from heterogeneous map behaviors and expresses them as prioritized natural language queries. It first learns from progressive reasoning demonstrations that synthesize user profiles and map histories for situation understanding, intent expansion, and query prioritization. We then introduce intent-aligned group relative policy optimization, using subsequent user interactions to reward query relevance and ranked service coverage while penalizing redundancy and excessive response length. A two-level credit assignment mechanism integrates shared list-level advantages with query-specific advantages, coordinating individual query quality with the complementary coverage of the complete query list. We further construct MILES-Bench from real user interaction logs on a large-scale mapping platform, supporting training and evaluation across diverse services under rich and sparse behavioral histories. Extensive experiments against general-purpose LLMs and specialized recommendation baselines demonstrate superior POI retrieval utility and strong service and semantic alignment, with consistent gains from behavioral policy optimization across four backbone scales.

title: Learning from Physical Experience:Context-Space Adaptation for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Recent multimodal foundation models exhibit strong perception, reasoning, and in-context learning capabilities, but translating these capabilities into physical action remains challenging. Through real-world experiments across diverse manipulation tasks, we find that ChatGPT-6-Astra, a state-of-the-art general-purpose reasoner, can serve as a physically actionable, context-responsive manipulation policy, demonstrating effective fine manipulation and spatial reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce LEXP, a harness for learning from physical experience through context-space adaptation. LEXP combines task-level planning with an experience module that interprets execution evidence, extracts and retains lessons with applicability conditions, and reuses relevant lessons to generate contextual feedback for subsequent actions. Model weights and the action interface remain fixed throughout. Across 12 real-world manipulation tasks, LEXP achieves $23/36$ successful trials (63.9\%), compared with $19/36$ (52.8\%) with memory alone and $2/36$ (5.6\%) for vanilla Astra. On three tasks, bread transfer, sort trash and toiletries, and retrieve drawer, removing planning reduces success from $7/9$ to $4/9$, while removing retained experience reduces it to $3/9$. Execution traces illustrate feedback-guided corrections and cross-episode reuse of an inspection strategy. Execution analyses illustrate how task structure and experience-derived feedback guide task progression, action correction, and experience reuse. These results support context-space adaptation as a practical mechanism for turning physical interaction into reusable guidance for robotic manipulation.

title: Existence, Equivalence, and Convergence of Unbalanced Optimal Transport
abstract: We study an unbalanced optimal transport problem with a spatially independent signed source. The target density is continuous on a bounded domain or continuous and integrable on $\mathbb R^n$. We establish sequential weak lower semicontinuity at the critical Sobolev regularity $W^{1,n}$ and existence of minimizers under prescribed distortion and Jacobian mass bounds, provided a finite-energy admissible pair exists. For domain-preserving, uniformly bi-Lipschitz affine flows, we prove an energy-preserving static-dynamic correspondence and stability of the reconstruction. Within this class, sequential $Γ$-convergence identifies the strong source-penalty limit as transport minimization among pairs of minimum source cost. This yields optimal-cost asymptotics and subsequential convergence of minimizers and their reconstructed paths. When a constant source is admissible, optimal sources converge strongly in $L^2$ to the constant determined by the endpoint mass difference. We establish local constant-source feasibility for Hölder endpoint densities near a fixed reference pair and give a quantitative obstruction showing that constant-source feasibility may fail even when admissible pairs exist.

title: Transferring Peptide-Target Interaction Patterns to Small Molecules by Joint Guidance for Diffusion and Flow Matching
abstract: Generating small molecules to target protein-protein interactions (PPIs) remains one of the most challenging yet high-reward frontiers in drug discovery. Unlike traditional small-molecule drugs that bind to deep, well-defined pockets, PPI interfaces often comprise broad, shallow binding surfaces. A natural strategy is to leverage known peptide-target interactions, as peptide ligands provide rich interface-level constraints. However, a major algorithmic challenge is that rigid atom-level conditioning on peptide structures can over-constrain the generative space and exclude valid small-molecule solutions. To address this challenge, we present PIFT (Peptide InterFace Transfer), a novel framework that transfers peptide-target interaction patterns to small molecules through joint sampling-time guidance of masked discrete diffusion and continuous flow matching. PIFT first maps peptide-target and small-molecule-target interfaces into a shared, target-conditioned interaction space, capturing transferable interface information across molecular modalities. The resulting peptide-derived reference then jointly steers building-block logits and 3D coordinates toward peptide-compatible molecules while preserving a strong adapted molecular prior. Extensive experiments across diverse PPI targets show that the learned representation captures cross-modal interaction compatibility, while peptide guidance improves interface recovery and achieves strong docking performance and favorable molecular properties.

title: OrionLink: Single Sign-On with Oblivious Identity Brokers
abstract: Single Sign-On (SSO) is a federated authentication mechanism that improves user experience by enabling access to multiple services, or Relying Parties (RPs), through a single authentication at an Identity Provider (IdP). To reduce integration complexity, many RPs rely on third-party Identity Brokers (Brokers) that aggregate numerous IdPs into a unified interface, thereby simplifying protocol management and interoperability. However, while brokers ease development, they introduce a fundamental security and privacy risk: sensitive authentication credentials and user behavioral data are exposed to the broker, creating a high-value single point of failure. Existing SSO solutions provide limited protection against these risks. With the goal of achieving broker obliviousness, we address these challenges at their root and present OrionLink, a comprehensive privacy-enhancing SSO pipeline that is compatible with existing brokered SSO architectures and systematically mitigates broker-induced risks without sacrificing usability. OrionLink incorporates two core components: (a) an anonymous pseudonym derivation scheme that generates unlinkable, per-RP identifiers to prevent cross-service user tracking; (b) an anonymous key exchange protocol that establishes end-to-end encrypted channels to protect user data from broker visibility. We further instantiate OrionLink with two new features, preserving broker functionality and deployability. We implemented a prototype of OrionLink within a brokered SSO environment, and experimental evaluation shows that the framework achieves substantial security and privacy improvements with acceptable performance overhead.

title: RapidDOC: Riccati-Preconditioned Implicit Differentiation for Differentiable Optimal Control under Operator Mismatch
abstract: Differentiable optimal control embeds constrained optimization problems in data-driven pipelines by differentiating their optimality conditions and propagating task-loss gradients to model or objective parameters. A key observation is that forward optimization and backward sensitivity computation involve related stage-structured linear systems, making reuse of forward factorization information natural. However, direct reuse is generally invalid, because differences in linearization, barrier terms, regularization, and curvature can create a mismatch between the retained forward operator and the target operator defining the derivative. We therefore propose RapidDOC, a factorization-reuse method that leaves the target adjoint equation unchanged. The retained cache produces a candidate adjoint and, when its target residual exceeds the prescribed tolerance, serves as a fixed right preconditioner for GMRES. A cache-action error operator characterizes directional exactness, the preconditioned iteration, and the relation between target residual and outer-gradient error. An ablation on three constrained robotic OCPs shows that the proposed method achieves lower backward time than both target-system refactorization and a no-reuse iterative method, demonstrating the computational benefit of reusing the retained forward factorizations. Across open- and closed-loop parameter-learning experiments, the proposed method achieves learning performance comparable to the baselines, while yielding the lowest open-loop backward time on all three tasks and reducing total closed-loop solver-call time by 40.5-83.1% relative to the fastest competing method. Finally, deploying the learned controller on a physical vehicle reduces the median figure-eight tracking RMSE from 22.75 to 6.09 cm, demonstrating its potential for hardware deployment.

title: A reciprocal Schoenberg inequality and its extensions
abstract: We study reciprocal moments of the critical points of a polynomial with a simple zero at the origin. A positive similarity transforms a reciprocal derivative companion into a complex symmetric matrix. This gives a short proof of the reciprocal Schoenberg inequality and a refinement for every elementary symmetric function. We determine the optimal constants in the corresponding inequalities for every positive exponent, including the sublinear range, and extend the results to arbitrary positive charges. We also characterize the normal powers of the companion and of its symmetric representative. The resulting criterion gives the complete equality cases in two quartic inequalities and explains the appearance of noncollinear equality configurations at higher orders. We also obtain a closed generating determinant and a quantitative collinearity estimate.

title: Exponential stability of port-Hamiltonian systems with unstructured, measurable Hamiltonian densities
abstract: For first-order port-Hamiltonian systems in the dissipative setting considered here, we characterise exponential stability without any further regularity or block-structure assumption on the Hamiltonian density, thus closing a gap persisting in the literature. The proof requires revisiting the computation of the adjoint generator of the port-Hamiltonian semigroup. Finally, we provide both examples and non-examples showcasing the inconclusiveness of known conditions on the Hamiltonian densities necessary for the application of characterisation results in the literature.

title: Agentic Global Optimization of Site-Disordered Crystalline Materials
abstract: Site-disordered crystals, in which several elements partially occupy the same atomic site, cannot be simulated atomistically without first resolving an explicit ordering, and the number of possible orderings grows combinatorially with supercell size. Because each candidate requires an expensive structural relaxation, locating the global-minimum ordering is a costly combinatorial search. Here, we present an agentic search in which a surrogate model, fitted to previously evaluated configurations, selects each subsequent candidate by balancing exploitation, uncertainty, and novelty. Four surrogates are implemented within a shared framework: an ExtraTrees ensemble, Bayesian ridge regression, sparse ARD regression, and an ALiEGNN-inspired graph ensemble. These are benchmarked against three traditional methods: random walk, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and a genetic algorithm across 14 test cases spanning 12 crystal structures, with exhaustively enumerated global minima as ground truth. The agentic surrogates reach the global minimum in 94% of runs, compared with 55% for the traditional methods, with a median 4.3-fold reduction in evaluations relative to the best traditional method. Bayesian ridge regression succeeds in all runs with the fewest evaluations. Applied to Na2/3FePO4, with coupled Na/vacancy configurational disorder and Fe2+/Fe3+ charge disorder, the framework recovers the experimentally reported ordering when charge states are encoded in the surrogate representation, demonstrating its extension to multi-sublattice disorder.

title: With foundation-model features, aggregator complexity does not improve cross-hospital discrimination in gastric whole-slide image classification
abstract: Whole-slide image classifiers are usually developed within one hospital and often go untested at unseen hospitals. We assembled 5,036 haematoxylin-and-eosin-stained gastric slides from five Korean hospitals, scanned at 20x and 40x, and compared multiple-instance learning aggregators under leave-one-hospital-out validation on frozen pathology foundation-model features. A hierarchical patch-region-slide graph aggregator (CHIME-MIL) with site alignment and two-scale fusion reached a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.837, above six conventional attention and transformer aggregators trained without these steps. Under a matched recipe it did not exceed attention-based pooling, and global max pooling given the same alignment and fusion was better (AUC 0.855, P = 0.0002). The alignment, which subtracts each hospital's mean feature vector without labels, onboarded a new hospital from ten unlabelled slides and cost 0.002 AUC without held-out-hospital data, but its accuracy gains were small and inconsistent. The model had low top-label calibration error (0.053) but under-confident malignancy probabilities, and removing its most-attended patches lowered the malignancy probability far more than removing random patches. With these features, more complex aggregators did not improve discrimination; what a deployable system adds is label-free onboarding, calibration checks and auditable evidence.

title: Integral Harnack-type estimates and the rate of extinction for nonlocal doubly nonlinear parabolic equations
abstract: We establish local boundedness and integral Harnack-type inequalities for locally nonnegative weak solutions to nonlocal doubly nonlinear parabolic equations in the fast diffusion range by combining refined energy estimates with a careful treatment of the nonlocal terms. As an application, quantitative decay estimates for both the local mass and the local supremum of weak solutions are derived near the extinction time. Furthermore, we study the extinction phenomenon for bounded nonnegative weak solutions to the Cauchy--Dirichlet problem and obtain quantitative upper bounds for the extinction time.

title: Cross-Embodiment Motion Planning by Coupling Body-Agnostic World Model with Differentiable Ego-Dynamics
abstract: Motion planning in clutter is embodiment-specific: the feasible free space and reachable commands depend on each robot's geometry and dynamics. Existing cross-embodiment policies output normalized commands that disregard these differences, or compensate through per-robot training and distillation. World models can in principle pool cross-embodiment data, yet command-conditioned models bind their latent dynamics to a single action space, while pose-conditioned models omit the mapping from commands to body-specific motion. On flat ground, however, embodiment affects the planner's observations only through the camera ego-motion. This letter proposes Hourglass, an hourglass-shaped architecture that factorizes cross-embodiment motion planning at this interface: a body-agnostic world model and each robot's differentiable ego-dynamics, which map commands to that ego-motion, are coupled only through it. The world model is trained on data pooled across embodiments and camera mounts; each robot's ego-dynamics is a reduced-order template with identified physical parameters. A generalist parameter-conditioned policy is learned once at this junction: each imagined step rolls out the template and then the world model, and imagination training through each robot's template makes the policy body-aware. On seven simulated robots of five locomotion types, the generalist policy outperforms imitation-learning and diffusion-policy baselines on the same world model by 3.8--10.6 percentage points in success rate and matches per-robot specialists without dedicated training, while approaching its parameter-conditioned MPPI teacher within 1.4--2.8 points without an online map. After three minutes of teleoperated driving for identification, the synthetic-data-trained model transfers zero-shot to a real skid-steer robot unseen in training, navigating unseen indoor scenes.

title: Region-Preserving Accelerated Gradient Methods for Geodesically Convex Optimization
abstract: Accelerated Riemannian optimization methods often require a priori assumptions that their iterates remain in a region where geometric bounds hold. We develop a parameterized inertial dynamical system and an explicit accelerated gradient method for smooth geodesically convex optimization on Riemannian manifolds with locally bounded sectional curvature. Our setting allows both positive and negative curvature without requiring completeness of the ambient manifold. Starting from a curvature-corrected continuous model, we construct the discrete updates by eliminating indefinite cross terms in the Lyapunov energy difference and derive verifiable conditions for a fixed step size. The resulting energy analysis establishes preservation of the initial geodesic ball without assuming iterate containment in advance. We further establish accelerated convergence rates for both geodesically convex and strongly geodesically convex objectives, without requiring restarts.

title: Kloosterman Sums and Plücker Height Zeta Functions
abstract: We establish nontrivial bounds for Kloosterman sums over $p$-adic fields associated with the longest Weyl element on arbitrary split reductive groups, at arbitrary level. As an application, we obtain the regularity of Bessel distributions (of Whittaker models) for all such groups.

title: StrictPRMBench: A Replayable Evaluation Benchmark for Auditing Fixed-Score PRM Aggregation
abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) score reasoning steps, but best-of-N selection also requires a rule that aggregates those scores. We study that rule as a separate evaluation object. StrictPRMBench fixes mathematical reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and the source trace of a deletion intervention, so that different reducers face the same recorded selection problem. Across seven scoring checkpoints and two benchmarks, the stored N=32 outcomes give higher deletion-induced selection instability for product than geometric mean (GM) in all 14 cells. The equal-cell difference is +0.0965; a shared-problem bootstrap, conditional on these checkpoints and frozen pools, gives a 95% interval of [0.0846,0.1086]. A pre-injection-defined sensitivity excludes replacement slots that are either reducer's clean winner and retains 4,459 of 4,622 cell-problem records. The retained difference is +0.0986 [0.0875,0.1098]. Effects are heterogeneous: the two Qwen cells have positive percentile-bootstrap intervals on retained support but two-sided exact paired p-values of 0.0625 and 0.0703. Clean-pool Qwen accuracy does not detect a product advantage, but this is not an equivalence result. We provide versioned outcome records, CPU reanalysis, and an explicit evidence-availability contract. The contribution is a diagnostic evaluation protocol and a reproducible audit of recorded selector behavior, not a new PRM, a universally optimal reducer, or evidence of deployment-wide harm. Raw-score replay and outcome-record reanalysis are distinguished: missing primary edited-score vectors limit independent evaluation of new reducers under the same stress.

title: HIPC: Humanoid Iterative Planning and Control via Goal-Conditioned Motion Closure
abstract: Recent generative models are widely used to provide whole-body motion for humanoid tracking. Current methods combine motion generators with controllers in an open-loop paradigm, which leads to critical issues: tracking errors can accumulate into spatial drift, and the planner cannot adapt to unexpected physical disturbances without feedback from physical execution. However, directly feeding realized states back to the planner in a closed loop can cause discontinuities, resulting in physical jitter and even falls, since such states are out of distribution during training. To bridge this gap, we propose HIPC, a real-time Humanoid Iterative Planning and Control framework that couples a generative model with motion tracking into a unified planning-and-control paradigm. HIPC introduces a goal-conditioned motion planning trained with a canonical motion representation that avoids gimbal-lock singularities under extreme orientations and supports motion generation on diverse geometric and semantic conditions. Then, HIPC adopts two strategies, deviation-decayed recovery and history re-anchoring, to mitigate the out-of-distribution shift caused by realized-state feedback. Finally, HIPC operates a real-time asynchronous planning-and-control system, with latency compensation to reduce temporal mismatch for inference delay. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of HIPC under switching and composition of diverse conditions. Results show that HIPC achieves state-of-the-art goal-reaching accuracy among existing methods while simultaneously demonstrating robustness to physical perturbations and the ability to recover from falls.

title: Pix2Evidence: A Multimodal RAG System for Text and Visual Evidence
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over visually rich documents must find both relevant content and the evidence that supports an answer. Screenshot retrieval preserves images and page structure, but written facts within screenshots also need to be searchable. Moreover, topical relevance alone does not identify which retrieved tile contains evidence for the answer. We introduce Pix2Evidence, a multimodal RAG system that encodes each screenshot tile together with its available transcription into a single fused image--text representation, so that layout and readable text are considered jointly during retrieval. To guide evidence selection, a vision-language teacher describes the visible content that supports each training question. We use these descriptions to adapt the retriever, then rerank the retrieved candidates before answer generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Pix2Evidence outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Across five widely-used Wikipedia QA benchmarks, the non-reranked Pix2Evidence leads the main comparison in answer accuracy on four. On MMSearch, it reaches 26.0\%, 4.4 percentage points above PixelRAG. We will release the code and share derived data where licensing and privacy reviews permit.

title: HandMimicX: Learning Human-Like Dexterous Manipulation via an Object-Centric Policy from Egocentric Videos
abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from human videos remains an open challenge, particularly in the context of transferring a single demonstration into a spatially generalizable robotic skill and maintaining physically plausible human-like interactions. Unlike prior works that emphasize hand-motion imitation, we introduce an object-centric framework for acquiring dexterous skills from egocentric human RGB-D videos. Within our framework, we formulate the reinforcement learning (RL) objective in terms of object motion to decouple the underlying skill from the specific hand trajectory and impose constraints on hand-object interaction states to promote more anatomically natural hand configurations. Extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate that our method enables efficient learning from human videos and generalizable skill transfer across novel spatial configurations.

title: Bayesian PET Reconstruction with Learned Flow Matching Priors via Langevin Sampling
abstract: Image reconstruction for positron emission tomography (PET) is a challenging inverse problem due to its inherent ill-posedness and Poisson counting noise, particularly in low-dose acquisitions. In this work, we introduce a novel Bayesian PET reconstruction framework that leverages a flow-matching generative prior learned from high-quality PET images. By incorporating this prior, we formulate PET reconstruction as a Bayesian inference problem and solve it via latent-space posterior sampling using the unadjusted Langevin algorithm. We evaluate the proposed method through numerical experiments and benchmark it against classical reconstruction methods and state-of-the-art deep learning-based baselines. The proposed method achieves improved reconstruction performance while enabling posterior uncertainty quantification.

title: PRIN: A Perceptual-Structural Retinex-Inspired Network for Low-Light Image Enhancement
abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) focuses not only on visibility recovery but also on preserving structurally meaningful content and perceptual naturalness. Existing learning-based methods may achieve favorable pixel-wise fidelity while still producing over-smoothed textures, color deviations, or spatially incoherent illumination. Retinex-inspired methods provide interpretable decomposition into reflectance and illumination components, however, the asymmetric restoration roles of these components are rarely encoded through branch-specific frequency-domain refinement. To address this issue, we propose a Perceptual-Structural Retinex-Inspired Network (PRIN), which integrates Retinex priors with restoration-role-aware enhancement. PRIN employs a shared encoder and asymmetric decoders to estimate reflectance and illumination components. The reflectance branch performs attention-guided and edge-aware wavelet refinement to preserve textures and boundaries, whereas the illumination branch promotes spatially coherent brightness adjustment. After the recomposition of reflectance and illumination branches, a curve-based post-composition enhancement head calibrates residual tone and exposure deviations. Experiments on LOL-v1, LOL-v2-Syn, and LOL-v2-Real show that the proposed network ties for the best structural similarity index (SSIM) and obtains the second-lowest learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) on LOL-v1, achieves the best SSIM and LPIPS on LOL-v2-Syn, and obtains the highest peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and the second-lowest LPIPS on LOL-v2-Real.

title: Updated $Σ_{c}$ excitation spectrum including the $2P$- and $1F$-wave fine structures
abstract: In order to study the new $Σ_{c}$ baryons observed by the LHCb collaboration recently, we update the previously predicted $Σ_{c}$ excitation spectrum by extending the excited states up to the highly excited $2P$- and $1F$-wave states. The calculation is performed in the framework of the relativized quark model and Gaussian expansion method by considering the mixing effect. The radially and orbitally excited states in the calculation are determined by the truncation convention proposed in this work and the mechanism of the heavy-quark dominance. The contribution of each Hamiltonian term to the energy levels is precisely calculated by using the two-step Gaussian expansion method. Then, the concerned $Σ_{c}$ states are obtained and the $Σ_{c}$ excitation spectrum including the $2P$- and $1F$-wave fine structures is established. Based on these, several important topics are discussed and analyzed, including the root-mean-square radii, off-diagonal matrix elements, mixing effect, fine structures and assignments of the newly observed $Σ_{c}(2800)^{0}$, $Σ_{c}(2900)^{0}$ and $Σ_{c}(3200)^{0}$ states. Meanwhile, it is found that the approximate decoupling phenomenon emerges in different $nL$-wave groups. This implies the reasonability of the truncation convention and is of great significance for further improving the calculation scheme for all the baryon spectra. Moreover, it is demonstrated that in the very high-lying $nL$-wave groups such as the $1F$-wave group, the energy level gaps become small even degenerate, and each of the baryon states has a big radius and therefore a loosely bound structure. In addition, by examining the experimental and calculated data, we suggest more precise experiments to search for more $Σ_{c}$ baryon states in the predicted $1P$- and $2P$-wave fine structures whose central energies are around 2822 and 3210 MeV, respectively.

title: Clique-factors in randomly perturbed hypergraphs
abstract: In this paper we establish the following result for clique-factors in randomly perturbed hypergraphs when the cliques are large enough. For integers $k \geq 3$ and $t\geq t_0(k)$, we show that for every $α> 0$, there exists $C>0$ such that for sufficiently large $n\in(t+1)\mathbb{N}$, the union of a $k$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices with minimum codegree at least $αn$ and a binomial random $k$-uniform hypergraph $H^{(k)}(n,p)$ with $p\geq Cn^{-{t/\binom{t+1}{k}}}$ on the same vertex set contains a $K_{t+1}^{(k)}$-factor asymptotically almost surely. The bound on $p$ is asymptotically best possible and extends the graph case, resolved by Balogh, Treglown and Wagner. In particular, we have $t_0(3)=3$, which implies that our result applies to every $t\ge 3$ for $3$-uniform hypergraphs. Together with the previously established result for perfect matchings, this covers all possible clique sizes for $3$-uniform hypergraphs.

title: Time-Domain Multiplexing for Resource-Efficient Heralded GKP State Preparation
abstract: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are key resources for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, but their conditional preparation via Gaussian boson sampling involves a trade-off between source count and photon-number resolution. Distributing heralding photons across more measured modes reduces the resolution required per mode, yet increases the number of simultaneously operated squeezed sources in fully squeezed spatial architectures. Here, we show that time-domain multiplexing (TDM) can reduce these physical source requirements while preserving GKP state quality. Using an end-to-end differentiable Bargmann framework, we find that TDM circuits reusing one or two squeezed sources achieve fidelities comparable to fully squeezed spatial circuits across several configurations. Selected nine-mode configurations retain fidelities above 0.95 with one photon heralded in each measured mode, mitigating detector resolution demands without a proportional increase in source count. Loss-aware reoptimization further shows that, under the investigated spatial loss models, two-mode TDM maintains fidelities near 0.80 at 1.0 dB per channel, whereas the corresponding spatial benchmarks fall below 0.60. These results demonstrate that temporal reuse provides an effective architectural route for balancing source overhead, detection demands, and state preparation performance in the presence of optical loss.

title: Efficient cross-domain multi-factor authentication
abstract: Secure cross-domain authentication is crucial for protecting information exchange across terminals in different security domains. However, existing cross-domain authentication models suffer from inflexibility, high storage and computational consumption. In response to these problems, a cross-domain multi-factor authentication protocol with improved efficiency (CDAuth) is proposed. CDAuth employs a universally applicable multi-factor authentication approach, integrating pseudo-identity, attribute concealment, and biometric hiding. The authentication information sets can be freely added or modified to accommodate various access scenarios. This boosts privacy, flexibility, and applicability compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, multi-edge servers as Certification Authorities (CAs) store only the union of terminal attributes and a verification token per user in their subdomains, instead of each user's attribute and biometric sets as in traditional schemes, significantly reducing storage consumption. Additionally, replacing the bilinear pairing operations with the native group operations, while maintaining security, significantly reduces computational consumption. Our analysis shows that CDAuth can resist common security attacks and is more efficient than the previous schemes.

title: Spectroscopic observations of periodic bursty ejections during a dome-spire-shaped jet
abstract: Context: The study investigates the complexity of the formation and evolution of a dome-spire-shaped jet (or anemone jet) that originated in an active region and was presumably driven by null-point magnetic reconnection. Aims: We aim to provide a quantitative estimation of multi-temperature plasma dynamics and physical parameters of the jet and its blob-like features, together with its temporal evolution in three-dimensional perspective. Methods: For this, we analyze unique sit-and-stare spectral (Si IV, Mg II k, and C II) and slit-jaw imaging 1400 Å and 2796 Å observations obtained with the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), with a slit uniquely positioned just above the assumed reconnection site. Co-observations taken with the Fast Imaging Solar Spectrograph of the Goode Solar Telescope in the chromospheric H$α$ and Ca II 8542.10 Å lines were also analyzed. These data are complemented by EUV imaging information from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory. Results: The IRIS observations reveal that the jet is formed by multiple periodic ($\sim$30 s) plasma ejections with blob-like appearance, each associated with strongly blueshifted Si IV 1402.77 Å transition-region emission reaching about $-300$ km/s. More importantly, the ejections are grouped into well-defined packets, each lasting approximately 3--5 min. In contrast, only a single Doppler component is observed in the chromospheric Ca II line. Multi-Gaussian decomposition of the Si IV line profiles reveals a highly accelerated plasma, with line-of-sight speed toward the observer increasing linearly from $\sim$30 to 112 km/s over 66 s, corresponding to an acceleration of 1.3 km/s$^2$. The kinetic energy release rate is estimated in the range of $\sim$1.0$\times10^{24}$--1.0$\times10^{25}$ erg\,s$^{-1}$.

title: Disconnectedness of stability manifolds and their geometric loci, and separation of braid orbits of semiorthogonal decompositions
abstract: This paper proves that the Bridgeland stability manifold $\mathrm{Stab}(X)$ has infinitely many connected components for general quintic threefolds, other general complete intersection Calabi--Yau threefolds, certain odd-dimensional Calabi--Yau varieties, and certain rational weak Fano varieties.
