title: Current Sheets and Magnetic Reconnection statistics by Solar Orbiter at few to tens of Ion Inertial Lengths I: Energy Dissipation
abstract: In this work, we study the turbulent origin of ion-scale Current Sheets (CSs) and the dissipation of energy via magnetic reconnection. We analyze 103 hours of high-cadence (4 samples/s) in-situ ion data from Solar Orbiter, collected between July 2020 and September 2022. We apply an automatic detection algorithm that finds current sheets (CSs) of thickness (length in the normal direction, $λ$) near the ion inertial length ($δ_i$), and classifies them as Alfvénic or reconnecting. We compile a catalog of 974 CSs of thickness in the range of few to 90 ion inertial lengths, of which 53 contain an ion reconnection jet. We estimate that Solar Orbiter spends $\sim 1 \%$ of the dwell time inside a CS of few to 90 $δ_i$ thickness, and 0.06\% inside a reconnecting CS of the same thickness range. By comparing these results with previous studies we estimate that the abundance of CSs and of Reconnecting CSs evolves with heliocentric distance ($r$) as $r^{-0.9}$ and $r^{-1.5}$, respectively. We estimate that magnetic reconnection dissipates $ε_{rec}\sim 30 \hspace{5pt} \text{J} \text{kg}^{-1} \text{s}^{-1},$ in the $\sim 1 - 40$ $δ_i$ scale-range, by assessing the amount of plasma that interacts with a reconnection exhaust. We show how the dissipation of turbulence energy cascade by magnetic reconnection at scales smaller than 90 $δ_i$ is more effective closer to the Sun, and decays as $r^{-3.6}$. The current density of Alfvénic CSs thicker than the ion inertial length presents scale invariance, obeying $J_0/J_A=0.9(λ/2δ_i)^{-0.71}$, suggesting that CSs generated locally from solar wind turbulence.

title: IGDA-ICMH: an Importance Guided Feature and Network Dual Adaptation Framework towards Image Compression for Machine and Human Vision
abstract: With the surge of machine vision applications, image compression for both machine and human vision (ICMH) has become an important research area. Existing studies mainly focus on task-specific adaptation or multi-task joint optimization, yet they often overlook the unequal contributions of different features and network layers to downstream machine vision tasks. To address this issue, we first quantitatively investigate the impact of different feature and network layers on machine vision performance, providing a principled understanding of their importance. Based on this analysis, an Importance Guided feature and network Dual Adaptation (IGDA) framework is developed for ICMH. It adopts implicit neural representation as the basic architecture and designs an efficient adaptation structure with both feature and network weight adaptation. An Importance-Guided Network Adaptation (IGNA) module is developed with a low-rank adaptation strategy to selectively adjust key network layers according to their importance in different tasks. An Importance-Guided Feature Adaptation (IGFA) module is developed with a low-rank and Kronecker product-based transform to explore the non-local property of the features in order to reduce the number of adaptation parameters. Extensive experiments on representative machine vision tasks, including image classification and object detection, demonstrate that our IGDA-ICMH framework achieves significantly better performance than the existing implicit neural representation-based methods for ICMH.

title: Localisation and delocalisation of the integer-valued membrane model
abstract: We study the integer-valued membrane model on boxes $[-L,L]^d\cap\mathbb{Z}^d$ with zero boundary conditions. We show that in dimension two the model is delocalised at sufficiently high temperature. More precisely, the variance at the origin is of order $L^2/β$, where $β$ is the inverse temperature. More generally, for every $ε>0$ and all sufficiently small $β>0$, the logarithm of each Laplace transform lies between $(1+ε)^{-1}$ and $1$ times its Gaussian counterpart. The temperature threshold is independent of $L$ and the test function. In dimensions three and four, we prove that the variance at the origin is bounded uniformly in the box size at every positive inverse temperature. Thus the integer constraint changes the order of fluctuations in these dimensions. The proofs use a modification of the Fröhlich--Spencer argument in dimension two and a comparison with integer-valued Gaussian free fields in higher dimensions.

title: Lifting the mixed to the pure: quantum phases of matter from canonical purification
abstract: Pure-state quantum phases are defined through finite-depth local unitary connections. This concept of phases has recently been generalized to mixed states in terms of locally reversible channels. In this work, we establish a fundamental relation between mixed-state phases and pure-state phases. We show that a locally reversible channel between mixed states can be lifted to a local isometry between their canonical purifications; thus, if two mixed states are in the same phase, then their canonical purifications are in the same pure-state phase. Furthermore, an explicit construction of the lifting isometry is given by ``half'' of the Petz recovery map, suggesting that the Petz recovery map \emph{without rotation} is enough to connect mixed state phases. We illustrate our results with two examples: toric code under bit flip noise and Chern insulator under fermion number noise.

title: Variance Reduction for Decentralized Stochastic Optimization with Multiple Local Updates
abstract: Multiple local updates are widely used in decentralized optimization to enhance communication efficiency, often in conjunction with stochastic gradients when exact gradient computation is costly. However, such algorithms generally converge only to a neighborhood of the optimum, whose size depends on the stepsize and the variance of gradient noise. Variance reduction has been incorporated into ADMM-based methods to achieve exact convergence in expectation, but their stepsizes typically scale inversely with both the square root of the network size and the cube of the number of local updates, leading to slow convergence as the network size or the number of local updates increases. In this paper, we propose a novel primal-dual-based decentralized optimization algorithm that integrates variance reduction with multiple local updates, with a stepsize independent of the network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates (rather than its cube), thereby enabling significantly larger stepsizes and faster convergence. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, we establish the first linear convergence guarantee in expectation for decentralized optimization with multiple local updates under stochastic gradients in the strongly convex setting. Beyond the theoretical guarantee, the proposed method exchanges only one variable per round, halving the communication cost compared with gradient-tracking-based methods. Numerical experiments further demonstrate its advantages in convergence speed and accuracy.

title: Inverse source problem for the stochastic fractional Helmholtz equation in inhomogeneous media
abstract: This paper is concerned with an inverse source problem for the stochastic fractional Helmholtz equation in a three-dimensional inhomogeneous medium. The source is modeled as real Gaussian spatial white noise with an unknown nonnegative strength function. For admissible frequencies, we establish well-posedness of the radiating solution in the distributional sense and show that it has a smooth representation outside the source region. For the inverse problem, by using two-point correlations of the field measured in an exterior open set at a single frequency, we prove a logarithmic stability estimate for recovering the source strength under an a priori Sobolev bound. As a uniform Hölder stability estimate is unavailable for the general admissible class, by assuming the difference between two source strengths has a fixed sign, we improve the stability to Hölder continuity with an optimal Hölder exponent. The analysis combines scattering theory and quantitative continuation for the fractional Laplacian using the Caffarelli-Silvestre extension.

title: Alcove walks, crystal structure and a Levi branching rule
abstract: In the Borel case $P=B$, we endow Haines' set of maximal-dimensional positively folded alcove walks (arXiv:2405.17174) with a crystal structure. We construct a bijection with the LS-gallery model of Gaussent and Littelmann (arXiv:math/0307122) and prove that it intertwines the root operators. This answers a question raised by Haines. We also extend the Gaussent-Littelmann stratification to the parabolic setting, prove the Levi branching rule for LS galleries, and compare the resulting gallery model with Haines' maximal-dimensional positively folded alcove walks in the parabolic setting.

title: Nonequilibrium Transient Centers in Continuous-Time Systems
abstract: Analysis of mathematical models in ecology and epidemiology often emphasizes asymptotic dynamics, such as stable equilibria, periodic orbits, and attractors. However, many biologically relevant trajectories exhibit long transient dynamics in which a relevant observable evolves slowly for an extended period before a comparatively rapid transition occurs. On finite time scales relevant to data collection, management, and intervention, such transient behavior can be more informative than the eventual asymptotic outcome. In this work, we study long-lasting and slowly varying transient dynamics in continuous-time systems through the framework of nonequilibrium transient centers. These centers are points in the state space near which the observable can remain nearly constant for a long time, even when the full state is not near an equilibrium. We develop finite-time escape criteria for identifying such centers and their reachable counterparts. These criteria provide practical conditions under which nearby trajectories can remain in a slow regime for a long period of time before eventually leaving it. We apply the theory to an epidemic model with delay of stability loss. In this model, trajectories may remain close to the disease-free manifold for a long time before the infectious population resurges. The framework developed here describes this behavior as slow evolution near a nonequilibrium transient center followed by finite-time escape from the slow regime.

title: A Tropical Viewpoint on the Nagata--Biran--Szemberg Conjecture
abstract: We give a tropical perspective on the recent arguments announced by OpenAI for Nagata's conjecture and the Nagata--Biran--Szemberg conjecture. By degenerating to both the normal cone and a semistable model whose dual graph is a cycle, we replace sections on a surface by Laurent polynomials in two variables. In place of theta functions, tropical methods bound the exponents of these Laurent polynomials, and a lift of the tropical Abel--Jacobi class of the normal bundle controls the shape of the resulting exponent diagram. Combining these support bounds with interpolation on a torus proves the Nagata--Biran--Szemberg conjecture with its predicted threshold whenever the corresponding linear series contains an integral curve whose only singularity is an ordinary node that is not a basepoint.

title: Generative Design and Graph Neural Network Screening of Novel Bimetallic Alloy Catalysts for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
abstract: Identifying earth-abundant catalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is a central challenge in scalable green hydrogen production. We present a computational pipeline that couples diffusion-based generative modelling, machine-learning force-field relaxation, and graph neural network (GNN) property prediction to discover bimetallic HER catalysts beyond the structures and stoichiometries covered by existing adsorption databases. A generative model (MatterGen) is fine-tuned on bulk alloy structures labelled with their minimum hydrogen adsorption energy and steered towards adsorption energies near zero. From the generated pool we retain the stable structures that are novel bimetallic alloys: binary compositions built from the training-set metals but at stoichiometries or structures absent from that database. Each candidate's low-index facets are ranked by a machine-learning-force-field (MatterSim) surface-energy screen, and only the most stable terminations are converted into explicit slab models with hydrogen adsorbed at all high-symmetry surface sites and relaxed with the same force field. Two GNN surrogates (MEGNet and ALIGNN), trained on a high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) dataset, then screen the resulting slab candidates. Because the two models encode the local environment through different inductive biases, we retain only the alloys on which both agree, reducing the influence of any single model. This consensus screening, combined with a MatterSim energy-difference triangulation, resulted in a shortlist of near-thermoneutral bimetallic candidates. Eight are validated with plane-wave DFT, and four of them, Pd5Au, Pt5Rh, Cu5Pt3, and Pd13Ru3, bind hydrogen within the thermoneutral window. All eight alloys are dynamically stable by phonon calculations. These four alloys are highlighted as DFT-validated bimetallic HER candidates for experimental follow-up.

title: Binary Sparse Codes: Where are we on Energy Efficient Representations?
abstract: Biological neural systems achieve impressive computational capabilities under tight metabolic constraints, relying on sparse cortical representations that minimise total neural activity. This combination of efficiency and representational power has motivated growing interest in sparse coding as a computational strategy for artificial systems. Artificial models designed to produce binary sparse codes span three broad paradigms, theoretical methods grounded in efficient coding, deep learning methods trained via backpropagation, and biologically plausible methods that learn through local Hebbian rules, each yielding codes whose quality depends not only on achieving low activation density but also on preserving the informational structure of the input. The latter property, however, lacks an agreed-upon quantitative definition, leaving the field without a principled basis for comparing methods. We propose a set of metrics that formalise information preservation as similarity preservation, measuring how faithfully a binary sparse code reproduces the relational geometry of the input space, and apply this framework to compare four representative methods under matched conditions. The results reveal a consistent trade-off in which models that achieve high information preservation do so at the cost of sparsity, while models approaching the uniformity of an optimal random sparse code tend to sacrifice it. Competitive Sparse Codes, a biologically plausible approach, is the only architecture to occupy a region of near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information preservation. These findings frame the simultaneous satisfaction of both factors as an open challenge for the field and provide a reusable evaluation framework for measuring progress toward it.

title: An exploration of in-band spectral index techniques for extended radio sources with EMU
abstract: Spectral indices are an effective way of differentiating between thermal and nonthermal sources of radio emission. Most often, spectral indices are determined using flux measurements taken over multiple observations with different instruments. Since these data are not always available, determining spectral indices from a single telescope observation is desirable. The reliability of these in-band spectral indices has not been well studied, particularly for extended sources. Here, we explore three different techniques for finding in-band spectral indices with the Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU), a radio southern sky survey being conducted with the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP). These methods include: (1) integrating fluxes in sub-bands, (2) temperature-temperature (T-T) plots, and (3) using the ratio of the Taylor terms produced in the imaging process. We apply these techniques to a selection of extended sources of radio emission, primarily supernova remnants (SNRs) and HII regions, and assess if the indices produced through these methods agree with the expected values. For the SNRs, we also compare the in-band results to broadband spectral indices determined using flux values obtained from published works. We examine whether and when the in-band techniques can differentiate between thermal and nonthermal sources. In general, we find the T-T plot method to be the most reliable across the range of source sizes and brightnesses studied for both SNRs and HII regions. The sub-band and Taylor term methods can be useful under certain conditions but cannot be considered as broadly reliable for extended sources.

title: Parametric inference for the average hazard approach in time-to-event analysis with sparse risk sets
abstract: The average hazard (AH) is a recently proposed model-free summary of an event-time distribution. Over a prespecified window $[0,τ]$, it equals the cumulative incidence probability at $τ$ divided by the restricted mean survival time at $τ$ and can be interpreted as a person-time incidence rate that does not depend on the censoring distribution. The difference and ratio of AHs from two groups, DAH and RAH, are between-group contrasts on absolute and relative scales without requiring proportional hazards. Existing nonparametric inference for AH and its contrasts is based on the Kaplan--Meier estimator of the survival function, and can become unreliable when risk sets become sparse or exhausted near $τ$, as may occur in stratified analyses. As a practical remedy, we investigate parametric AH inference using Weibull and generalized gamma models. We use maximum-likelihood estimators and corresponding confidence intervals for group-specific AHs, DAH and RAH in both unstratified and stratified analyses. Simulations show that under correct model specification, little bias and near-nominal coverage can be achieved in settings where nonparametric inference is inadequately supported by observed data. We illustrate the method using a randomized trial comparing neratinib plus capecitabine with lapatinib plus capecitabine in metastatic breast cancer. Parametric inference provides a practical complement to nonparametric AH analysis when sparse or exhausted risk sets make inference at clinically relevant truncation times less reliable.

title: Adaptive Coverage Algorithms for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks in Dynamic Worlds
abstract: This paper extends an existing framework for the coordination of mobile agents in unknown worlds, by considering the possibility of dynamic instability. In the original problem, known as the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem (POCGAGP) (arXiv:2512.09495), the multi-agent system must establish a communication network which completely covers an initially unknown constrained space. However, the POCGAGP fails to account for the unpredictability often seen in real-world deployment. To address this, the dynamic case (DPOCGAGP) introduces two settings which can influence the mobile network during deployment: Agent Loss and World Change, which represent dynamic changes to the world. Within this study, we present advancements to two state-of-the-art algorithms, the Centralized Agent-Directed Exploration for Network Coverage (CADENCE), and its decentralized analogue, DADENCE, to provide solutions in these cases. We then compare their performance against another state-of-the-art benchmark algorithm, and show that the adapted algorithms outperform across our benchmark test set, which comprises over 4500 test cases of varied size and structure.

title: A Semiparametric Model Approach to Data Integration under Missing Not at Random
abstract: Integrating probability and non-probability samples requires accounting for an unknown selection mechanism that may depend on the outcome. We develop a semiparametric approach in which an unspecified function captures covariate dependence and a scalar tilting parameter governs outcome dependence. Identification follows from an instrumental-variable exclusion restriction and conditional completeness; a zero tilt gives a restricted missing-at-random submodel. We profile out the covariate component and construct cross-fitted, Neyman-orthogonal estimating equations for both the tilting parameter and the finite population mean. The resulting orthogonalized mass-imputation estimator supports centered root-N inference under nuisance product-rate conditions. Its linearization variance accounts for the probability sampling design and estimation of the tilting parameter. Simulations illustrate the cost of flexibility under correct parametric specification, protection against misspecification of the covariate component, and the consequences of invalid instruments or a misspecified tilt. A further simulation using 50,000 national health-screening records finds smaller bias but higher root mean squared error than a parametric competitor under the baseline instrument set. The proposed estimator varies less across alternative instrument sets, although weak instruments and smoothing choices affect precision and interval coverage.

title: Existence of the thermodynamic limit for the Hopfield model
abstract: We prove that the quenched pressure of the Hopfield model with $K\simαN$ i.i.d. symmetric Rademacher patterns has a thermodynamic limit at every load $α\in(0,\infty)$, finite inverse temperature and uniform external field, with no replica-symmetry, order-parameter concentration or non-condensation hypothesis required. The limit is the supremum over $r$ of limiting pressures of mixed models with $r$ binary patterns in a Gaussian bulk. Via the Hubbard--Stratonovich representation we extract the finitely many patterns whose hidden coordinates exceed $δ\sqrt N$; a collective interpolation replaces the other binary patterns by Gaussian ones with error $O(δ^2)$ uniform in the volume, and convex concentration on the discrete cube controls the disorder-dependent choice of retained patterns. For the mixed models we prove a Gaussian hidden-spin truncation bound uniform in the volume and in an arbitrary Ising potential, and convergence for Gaussian bulks with finitely many site-field types, reducing to results of Ho and of Chen, Ho and Issa on non-convex vector spin glasses with compact spins. For Gaussian patterns we give an alternative proof of the existence result announced by Camilli, Contucci and Mingione, extended to a uniform field and an extra binary pattern. In both cases the pressure has exponentially small deviation probabilities and converges a.s.; internal energy and entropy converge wherever the limit is differentiable. An extra binary Mattis pattern admits a scalar variational reduction. At zero field the Rademacher pressure dominates the Gaussian one with an extra binary pattern, which dominates the pure Gaussian one. No explicit formula is given. The proofs were generated through extensive interaction with the AI models Claude (Opus~5.5) and ChatGPT (Sol~6.1), based on the problem formulation and guidance of the authors.

title: Observable-Specific Validity Tests for Scientific AI: Controlled Approximations and Intervention Response
abstract: An approximation can reproduce an energy while missing its response, or satisfy an error tolerance without being certified by a given bound. We formulate observable-specific validity records for scientific artificial intelligence (AI) that link a reduction to its reference model, error measure, tolerance, parameter domain, and transformations or interventions. Explicit displacement and velocity certificates for a singularly perturbed oscillator recover distinct convergence orders and provide sufficient validity guarantees. Exact Hubbard dimer relations resolve the different coupling domains accepted by energy and response criteria. Across 16 repeated neural fits, imposing dimensional homogeneity reduces energy scale transfer error from 52.3% to 0.0768% and raises the median fraction jointly satisfying gap and response tolerances from zero to 100%. Paired transformations verify the protected scaling relation, while a coupling crossover identifies the additional information needed for response transfer. A causal model recovers a positive intervention response beneath a strong negative observational association. For two mechanisms observed with Gaussian noise whose responses first differ at order $x^k$, we derive an exact fixed control query requirement scaling as $x^{-2k}$ and verify its full success curve numerically. Together with a 256-task evaluation interface, these results provide independently checkable tests of controlled approximation, physical transfer, and mechanism discrimination in scientific AI.

title: Cosmology with post-EoR 21 cm Intensity Mapping surveys: power spectrum measurements in the last decade
abstract: The technique of 21 cm intensity mapping (IM) is emerging as a possible, cost-effective method to supplement optical surveys to map the large-scale structure, and extend their redshift reach, with projects aiming to cover a large range of post-EoR redshifts, from z=0 to z=6. Since the early discussions 20 years ago, a few dedicated interferometers have been built, and surveys have been carried out using them as well as general purpose radio instruments. An introduction to late-time cosmology with 21 cm intensity mapping is given, highlighting the main scientific and technical challenges. We present then an overview of different instrument concepts and survey strategies, followed by a discussion of outstanding data analysis challenges, most notably the foreground subtraction, which is a major issue in IM. We carry on with a presentation of the currently active projects and the 21 cm signal measurements which have been obtained, either in cross-correlation with optical surveys, or as the autocorrelation power spectrum. Finally, we discuss briefly the prospects for this field with future instruments and surveys such as SKA, HIRAX and CHORD.

title: Type classifiers
abstract: We extend dependent type theory by type classifiers and construct an interpretation in the category of contextual categories with families. Type classifiers extend contexts by type variables, complementing the usual context extensions by term variables of specified types. This allows statements with arbitrary type parameters to be formulated without assuming a universe. We show that substituting isomorphic types induces isomorphisms between the resulting types even in extensional type theory, giving an analogue of the invariance supplied by the univalence axiom in homotopy type theory. Omitting function types from the theory, so that all type formers are covariant, extends this naturality to arbitrary, possibly noninvertible maps.

title: Penetration of a sphere in a pool: Secondary pinch-off
abstract: The water entry of solid bodies, in particular spheres, has been the subject of numerous studies due to its relevance in multiple applications, especially focusing on cavity dynamics and the resulting forces and subsequent trajectories. The role of wettability in cavity formation and sustainability has been experimentally and theoretically addressed in the past; however, typically only up to the occurrence of a primary air cavity pinch-off. What is less explored is how wettability can influence higher-order pinch-offs. In the following study, especially secondary pinch-offs are shown to determine whether a sphere trajectory is terminally ascending, i.e., the sphere returns to the surface, or terminally descending: wettability is shown to be a strong influencing factor. This study begins with a series of systematic experiments, comparing the entry and trajectory of spheres over a range of impact Reynolds and Froude numbers, but also with varying surface wettability. From time resolved trajectories, a force balance is computed, illustrating the role of buoyancy, arising from the volume of any sustained air cavity in the wake of the sphere. Secondary pinch-offs alter this volume; hence, the terminal trajectory. A force-scale comparison and local radial balance at the cavity neck are then presented, suggesting how wettability influences the secondary pinch-off.

title: Epidemic Forecasting and Behavioral Response Estimation with a Behavior-Coupled SEIR Model
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has exhibited multiple waves of infections, reflecting feedback between disease transmission and adaptive population behavior. Accurately predicting and understanding these dynamics remains a central challenge for epidemic modeling. In this paper, we develop a forecasting framework based on a Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered (SEIR) model coupled with an evolutionary model of behavioral adaptation, in which population compliance with protective measures evolves in response to perceived infection risk and associated costs. We formulate forecasting as the estimation of behavioral incentive parameters that govern the coupled behavior-disease dynamics, using hospitalization time series data together with standard assumptions on disease-related parameters. Using the inferred parameters, we generate rolling monthly forecasts of infection levels and evaluate the approach on both synthetic data and hospitalization time series from multiple U.S. states (Texas, California, Colorado, and Arizona). The proposed framework provides a principled way to incorporate behavior-disease feedback into epidemic forecasting while yielding interpretable estimates of population-level incentives.

title: Locality, Probability and the Relevance of History
abstract: Relativistic theory and experiments teach us that causal influences are constrained by the speed of light. Deterministic theories incorporate this lesson in $\textit{functional}$ terms: whether an event occurs or not is functionally determined by events that occur in its immediate causal past. In this paper we suggest a natural generalization of this constraint that applies to probabilistic theories: the $\textit{probability}$ that an event occurs is to be functionally determined by the $\textit{probability}$ of the event-occurrences in its immediate causal past. This constraint differs from Bell's criterion of local causality and turns out to imply it only under an additional assumption that requires history to be, in a sense, $\textit{ir}$relevant. Bell-inequality-violating quantum phenomena are thus arguably $\textit{not}$ in tension with relativity, locality, "statistical independence", nor with a supposed "realism". What they instead show is that history is, in a sense, $\textit{relevant}$.

title: Optimal Average Distortion for Non-Expansive Embeddings of Euclidean Metrics into the Line: With applications to cut-matching games and vertex expansion
abstract: We show that any $n$-point Euclidean metric admits a non-expansive embedding into the line with average distortion at most $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}}\right)$, matching a known lower bound. We also present two applications of this result. First, we give a cut-player strategy with an optimal spectral guarantee for the undirected cut-matching game. Second, we give an improved spectral approximation for vertex expansion in high-degree graphs.

title: Sensorium: An Open-Source Multimodal Data Collection and Curation Library for Embodied Surgical AI
abstract: Embodied surgical AI requires reliable multimodal data, yet surgical data collection remains costly, difficult to repeat, and strongly dependent on the hardware setup. We present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data from configurable robot and sensor streams using the Robot Operating System (ROS) and ROS2 middleware. The library combines operator-facing data acquisition, configurable processing, semantic annotation, and episodic dataset generation. We evaluate Sensorium across 1516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments involving multiple surgical tasks and sensing configurations, and report preliminary usability feedback.

title: Turbulence on Hybrid Lattices: regular grids meet self similar cascade models
abstract: Turbulent cascades in high Reynolds number regimes span many decades in scale, which can be challenging for numerical simulations. Cascade models that use logarithmic discretization can help, but these have limited capabilities to describe spatial structures or real space details. Hybrid Lattices (HLs) are proposed in order to provide a novel framework to investigate turbulent cascades in Fourier space, combining regular grids and cascade models based on logarithmic discretisations. The approach consists of a regular spectral region, capable of resolving large scale coherent structures, that is extended in a recurrent, asymptotically self similar fashion, spanning many decades in scale. The idea comes from shell models and their extensions, namely the logarithmic lattices, the nested polyhedra models or the spiral chain models. The logarithmic spacing factor of those models, such as the golden ratio, typically prevents interactions between a regular grid and a self similar model. HLs are constructed by expanding a regular region in Fourier space through recurrence relations (e.g. the Fibonacci recurrence relation), generating an asymptotically logarithmic lattice where Cartesian components remain integer multiples of the regular Fourier space grid spacing. This way, the resulting grid preserves triadic interactions linking regular and recurrent regions, allowing energy transfer across these different regions. However, the sharp reduction in triads connecting the two regions creates a bottleneck effect, and in order to address this issue, a region of ghost points at the boundary had to be introduced, efficiently allowing the flux to leak into the recurrent part. The HL framework is then tested for the one dimensional Burgers equation, and for two dimensional incompressible Navier Stokes turbulence.

title: Formation of Micron-sized Presolar Graphite Grains in Low-energy Supernova Ejecta
abstract: Presolar graphite grains with supernova isotopic signatures provide direct evidence that large graphite grains formed in supernova ejecta. However, theoretical calculations of dust formation in supernovae have typically predicted graphite grains smaller than $0.1\,{\rm μm}$, leaving unclear the physical conditions required to form those grains with radii of order $1\,{\rm μm}$. We systematically investigate graphite nucleation and growth in expanding supernova ejecta by varying the explosion energy, ejecta mass, initial ejecta radius, and ejected $^{56}$Ni mass. We use a simplified one-zone model that follows the temperature and density evolution including adiabatic cooling, radiative cooling, and heating by radioactive nickel. We show that the final graphite grain size is mainly determined by the product of the mass density of atomic carbon available for grain growth and the local cooling timescale, both evaluated at a reference temperature of $2000\,{\rm K}$. Our models show that graphite growth is favored by lower explosion energy, larger ejecta mass, and smaller initial ejecta radius, which keep the gas denser near the graphite-condensation temperature. When radioactive heating and radiative cooling are included, explosions with $E_{\rm exp}\sim10^{50}\,{\rm erg}$ and $M_{\rm Ni}\lesssim10^{-3}\,M_\odot$ can form $1$-$10\,μ{\rm m}$ graphite grains in the ejected helium layer or carbon-oxygen core, whereas $E_{\rm exp}\sim10^{51}\,{\rm erg}$ models do not. These results suggest that micron-sized presolar supernova graphite preferentially forms in faint-supernova-like explosions with low explosion energies, little ejected nickel, and helium layer or carbon-oxygen core ejecta.

title: Optimizing Stochastic Policy Geometry for Few-Step Flow Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Few-step flow models generate samples through a handful of large denoising transitions. Applying GRPO to such models requires introducing stochasticity into the denoising transitions, and when a single transition spans a wide range of noise levels, the choice of the resulting stochastic policy becomes a major factor in optimization. Recent constructions constrain the policy to preserve the target flow coefficients, but this constraint admits a family of policies and offers no criterion for choosing among them. We introduce Geo-FSRL (Geometry-Optimized Few-Step Reinforcement Learning), built on a selection principle: at a fixed conditioning state and timestep pair, choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any given nonzero velocity-output update. Within a coefficient-preserving family of isotropic Gaussian transitions, this criterion reduces to minimizing a single scalar geometry factor that determines the conditional KL for every velocity-output update. The same factor governs velocity-space Fisher information and conditional transition log-likelihood-ratio variance. We derive the unique closed-form optimizer within this family, shared across all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, with transition coefficients determined by both the source and target noise levels. Because the minimized geometry factor still varies across timesteps, we further adopt gradient-scale matching from prior work and derive closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights that normalize explicit score scales and reference-KL curvature. Geo-FSRL trains on the original few-step schedule and retains the deterministic solver at inference. Our method achieves higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image generation and video generation models under the 4-step setting. Code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/lightx2v_rl

title: Strong edge-colourings of truncations of cubic graphs
abstract: We study a problem posed by Kardoš asking whether the truncation of every connected simple bridgeless cubic graph has strong chromatic index six. The truncation $T(G)$ is obtained by replacing each vertex of $G$ with a triangle and attaching its incident edges to distinct vertices of that triangle. An affirmative answer was previously established for prism bases by Han and Cui. We prove that $\sidx(T(G))=6$ whenever $G$ is a connected simple cubic graph that is bipartite or is both bridgeless and claw-free. Both proofs are constructive and use a common compatibility criterion for combining colourings of smaller pieces. The bipartite result also extends to non-det-extremal multigraphs.

title: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.

title: Thermal conductivity of Lennard-Jones fluids from equilibrium thermodynamics
abstract: We derive a general expression for the thermal conductivity of simple fluids within a thermodynamic transport theory (TTT) in which the Onsager coefficients of an interacting system are related to those of an ideal reference system through the ratio of the determinants of the Hessians of the relevant thermodynamic potential. The transported quantity is identified with an effective energy density proportional to the rms energy fluctuations of a small fluid cell. The result expresses the thermal conductivity as the product of its dilute-gas value and a function of equilibrium thermodynamic properties, namely the specific heats at constant density and at constant $ρT$ and the temperature derivative of the latter, with no adjustable parameters. For hard spheres, it reduces to a previously verified expression in terms of the thermodynamic factor. The theory is tested against molecular dynamics results for the Lennard-Jones (LJ) and the truncated and shifted Lennard-Jones (LJTS) fluids in the supercritical region, for densities up to $ρ^*=0.8$, using equations of state based on perturbation theory. For the LJTS fluid, the mean absolute percentage error is below 8\% for all the temperatures considered. For the LJ fluid, the predictions are compared with those of the revised Enskog theory for Mie fluids, using the same equation of state: TTT gives smaller errors at almost all temperatures, with a significant improvement at low temperatures, where the errors are reduced approximately by a factor between two and three.

title: Topological Multi-Natural Inflation
abstract: We investigate topological inflation in minimal multi-natural inflation, in which the axion potential consists of two cosine terms. Focusing on the high-scale regime, we perform a systematic parameter scan for representative ratios of the two periods and identify regions consistent with current constraints on the scalar spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio, including those from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. The interplay of the two harmonics allows departures from the quartic hilltop limit and accommodates the higher spectral index favored by recent cosmological data combinations. We characterize the hilltop and near-inflection-point branches and analyze the associated vacuum structure and domain-wall properties. We also discuss a symmetry-breaking origin of the required domain walls when the inflaton is the angular component of a complex scalar field. We identify regions in which the observational constraints and the adopted criteria for topological inflation are simultaneously satisfied, including regions with a sub-Planckian axion decay constant. Our results show that the observational tension encountered in the minimal quartic double-well model need not extend to topological inflation in a minimal multi-natural axion potential.

title: The metric Zariski multiplicity conjecture in dimension 4
abstract: Recently, OpenAI announced a counterexample to the Zariski multiplicity conjecture in dimension 4. Here, we prove that the metric Zariski multiplicity conjecture is true in dimension 4. More precisely, let $f,g\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$ be germs of reduced holomorphic functions, and let $φ\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ be a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism such that $φ(V(f))=V(g)$. We prove that if every irreducible component of the tangent cone of $V(f)$ at the origin has a singular locus of dimension at most two, then $V(f)$ and $V(g)$ have the same multiplicity at the origin. In particular, the multiplicity of complex analytic hypersurface singularities in $\mathbb{C}^n$, $n\leq 4$, is an embedded bi-Lipschitz invariant; the cases $n=2$ and $n=3$ were known. This extends a previous result of the author for tangent cones whose components have singular loci of dimension at most one. We also prove that two irreducible homogeneous hypersurfaces whose singular loci have dimension at most two, and which are mapped onto each other by a homeomorphism of $\mathbb{C}^n$ fixing the origin, have the same degree.

title: Shock Loading Accesses Reaction Pathways beyond Accelerated Thermolysis
abstract: Thermolysis and shock loading can produce similar major stable products in energetic materials, despite different chemical evolution and reaction pathways. Here, we develop EMFF-MACE, a reactive machine-learning potential for C/H/N/O energetic materials, enabling thermolysis simulations of 20 materials and shock simulations of 10 on a common potential energy surface. Comparisons at matched normalized reaction progress reveal divergent chemical states and local structural environments. Mean reaction-state similarity decreases from 94.0% at 20% progress to 25.9% at trajectory endpoints, while 47.1-92.6% of shock local environments lie outside corresponding material-specific thermolysis reference domains. Structural and reaction-network analyses reveal enhanced intermolecular reorganization and additional association and rearrangement branches under shock loading, despite partially shared early decomposition chemistry. These findings show that loading history influences the structural states and subsequent reaction pathways accessed during decomposition, rather than merely the rate of thermolysis.

title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting
abstract: Accurate forecasting with uncertainty quantification is critical in a variety of scientific applications ranging from epidemiology and economics to energy systems and earth sciences. Yet most forecasting models still need to be developed and trained separately for each domain-specific dataset. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to remove this limitation and enable the application of the same model across domains through large-scale pretraining. However, most existing TSFMs treat each time series independently and therefore cannot model interactions among time series and external drivers. Here, we introduce Chronos-2, a foundation model for zero-shot forecasting that models the interactions between multivariate time series and heterogeneous covariates, which commonly arise in scientific applications. The model infers relationships among time series directly from historical context and generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific treatment. Across various benchmarks, Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on average by improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points relative to the strongest baselines and increasing win rates by 10 percentage points. Chronos-2 is also computationally efficient, generating forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU, 50x and 1000x faster end-to-end than the best task-specific point and probabilistic forecasters, respectively. In addition, we demonstrate its effectiveness in diverse scientific settings -- including infectious-disease forecasting, macroeconomic modeling, carbon-flux prediction, and runoff simulation -- where the model matches or surpasses specialized methods developed for each domain. These results show that a single pretrained model can capture structure shared across temporal systems.

title: GENIE: learned quantum circuits as embedding impurity solvers, and why compactness, not correlation strength, decides when they work
abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization has been used as an impurity solver in density matrix embedding theory (DMET), but always with fixed-form circuits and without comparison to classical selection at the same subspace size. We introduce GENIE, a DMET impurity solver in which a generative transformer learns the sampling circuit, trained on the quantum-selected configuration interaction energy. On N2, hydrogen chains, water and a hydrogen ring, we compare GENIE at equal determinant budget with classical selected configuration interaction (CIPSI, ASCI, heat-bath CI) and with DMET combined with sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). GENIE selects: for N2 at 200 determinants it is within a factor of 1.7 of CIPSI and 25 to 1000 times more accurate than the determinants a fixed circuit actually samples, while standard SQD reaches good energies mainly by filling the subspace. GENIE does not beat the best classical selection, and its circuits require fault-tolerant hardware. Its failures are governed by the compactness of the wavefunction relative to the budget, not by correlation strength. A cheap estimate from coupled-cluster amplitudes predicts this compactness. A router built on it never recommended GENIE where it then failed, apart from seed-to-seed variance, and it transferred unchanged to a blind test on new systems. We also identify two benchmarking pitfalls that can create apparent quantum advantages of one to two orders of magnitude.

title: WASABI: Wasserstein Sampling via Bridge Interpolants
abstract: Sampling from Boltzmann distributions is a fundamental problem in physics, chemistry, and biology. We introduce WAsserstein SAmpling via Bridge Interpolants (WASABI), a method that trains a diffusion model to generate samples from a target Boltzmann distribution given access only to the energy function. WASABI minimizes the KL divergence between the distribution generated by its diffusion model and the Boltzmann target using Wasserstein gradient flows. This approach builds on a principle underlying classical sampling methods such as Langevin dynamics. However, applying Wasserstein gradient flows to diffusion models is challenging because the updates require the gradient of the model's own log density, which is generally intractable. We derive a practical training algorithm that avoids computing this gradient. Once trained, WASABI can generate new samples without further evaluations of the energy or its gradient. On alanine dipeptide, WASABI outperforms the best reported baselines using an estimated 3.3 times fewer energy evaluations. It also achieves competitive performance on interacting particle system benchmarks.

title: Compound drop impacts on substrates of different temperatures
abstract: In this paper, we report the impacts of isothermal compound drops for various combinations of viscous fluids. We extend an existing parameter-free model based on kinematic closure of drop impact to predict the maximum spreading diameter of both the core and the shell of compound drops. Then, we report impacts of compound drops on a cold surface. By using two liquids with different melting/freezing temperatures, it is possible to freeze either one of the two liquids or both and doing so, different patterns of frozen drops are obtained.

title: Neutrino Oscillation in a Static Dihole Geometry
abstract: We investigate neutrino flavor oscillations in the static equal-mass Majumdar-Papapetrou dihole geometry, restricting the propagation to the symmetry plane. Within the null approximation, we derive the leading contribution to the neutrino phase and numerically evaluate the geodesic integrals. For two neutrino flavors, interference between different trajectories introduces a dependence on the individual neutrino masses and on the neutrino mass ordering for nonmaximal mixing. We analyze the transition probability in different spacetime configurations possessing two light rings, a merged light ring (critical configuration), and no light rings in the equatorial plane. In the weak-lensing regime, the transition probability generally increases with the black holes' individual masses, while variations in the half-separation produce no qualitative change in the transition probability. In stronger-lensing configurations, variations in both the mass and half-separation modify the heights and positions of the extrema, with no monotonic increase or decrease in the transition probability. For the critical and no-light-ring configurations studied, we identify three zero-winding trajectories connecting the source and detector, including one passing near the symmetry axis. The probability remains oscillatory, and its oscillatory pattern depends strongly on the neutrino energy.

title: Robust Learning of Multi-Index Models under Logconcave Distributions via Weak Partial Learners
abstract: We develop a new algorithmic framework for learning Boolean concept classes under logconcave distributions. Our framework applies to broad families of multi-index models and yields significantly faster robust learners than were previously known in these settings. It extends to partial classification and testable learning. Consequently, we obtain improved learners for several fundamental concept classes, including functions of halfspaces and multiclass linear classifiers, under logconcave marginals. Our starting point is a new boosting framework based on weak partial learners. Classical boosting approaches require often-intractable distribution-free weak learners or yield weak approximation guarantees. We show instead that weak learners for partial classification, where labels may be undefined on part of the domain, suffice for strong agnostic learning. The key challenge is that boosting requires a weak learner that succeeds under conditioned distributions that are not guaranteed to be logconcave. To address this, we develop a recursive moment-based partitioning procedure: given a logconcave distribution $X$ and a conditional version $X'$, we partition the space into polynomially many convex regions so that, on most regions, the low-degree moments of $X$ and $X'$ approximately agree. On each good region, a well-behaved multi-index model correlates with a low-degree polynomial, giving a weak hypothesis. Combining these hypotheses yields the required weak learner. A key ingredient of our approach is an efficient method for detecting moment discrepancy. Specifically, we show how to find a low-dimensional subspace that captures any non-trivial discrepancy between $X$ and $X'$, if one exists. Our approach combines spectral analysis of moment tensors with recent progress on isoperimetry for logconcave measures. This discrepancy-finding procedure may be of independent interest.

title: When Is a Game a Markov Decision Process? Correspondences Between Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning and game theory describe the same object from two sides. Game theory says what a rational outcome of a strategic interaction is; reinforcement learning says how an agent could reach one through experience. The two literatures nevertheless keep separate vocabularies for identical structures, and the treatments that bridge them present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem. This monograph supplies the theorems. A game is a Markov decision process in three distinct senses, and every table entry is labelled with the one that applies: a definitional identity, an exact reduction carried by a value- and solution-preserving map, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions. We take every standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, extensive-form with imperfect information, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, and identify for each the decision-theoretic model that reinforcement learning already studies under another name. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts: Nash equilibrium and the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, quantal response equilibrium and the soft Bellman operator, the Shapley value and credit assignment, Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning. We map each model class onto the training procedures sound for it and record the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.

title: Zero Crossings on the Accuracy-Smoothness Frontier: Maximal Monotone and Minimal Inflection Non Stationary Predictors
abstract: The Smooth Sign Accuracy (SSA) framework resolves the smoothness--accuracy dilemma for stationary predictors by balancing mean squared error (MSE) against the frequency of sign changes. We generalize it to non-stationary integrated processes (I-SSA), deriving MSE-optimal predictors constrained by the expected duration between turning points (I(1)) or inflection points (I(2)). The resulting maximal-monotone and minimal-inflection predictors, filters, and smoothers customize classic benchmarks along a new efficient Accuracy--Smoothness (AS) frontier. Tracking the identity (the original data) along this frontier defines the \emph{I-SSA trend}, a novel smoothing concept that, unlike classical filters, imposes no artificial structure on the data-generating process and is directly interpretable through explicit control of turning- or inflection-point frequency. The optimization is a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) that reduces to a Generalized Trust Region Subproblem (GTRS) with hidden convexity. On its feasible, invertible region the problem is convex with a well-defined global optimum, and an exact closed-form expression delivers the efficient AS frontier. Under fairly general assumptions, finite-sample solutions converge to an asymptotic I-SSA predictor, devoid of integration boundary perturbations. The framework unifies mean squared error on non-stationary levels, and sign accuracy, zero-crossing frequency, and target correlation on stationary differences.

title: No generalised contextuality from the vacuum
abstract: We show that, under certain conditions, generalised contextuality, in the sense introduced by Spekkens, cannot be created from the vacuum of a quantum field. Initial noncontextual qudit states do not become contextual just by interacting with a quantum field. This is verified in two scenarios. First, in a perturbative approach where the time evolution operator is expanded in powers of the coupling constant. Second, in the limit of zero energy gap in the spectrum of the free detector Hamiltonian. Our results are at the opposite side of what has been recently obtained in the literature regarding the harvesting of Kochen-Specker contextuality. Our results demonstrate that the existing notions of contextuality can be independent of one another and that contextuality harvesting depends on which precise notion is used.

title: Microswimmers lose by swimming selfishly
abstract: At low Reynolds number, microswimmers are coupled by the flows they create, even when they are apart. The best way for each swimmer to push itself forward then depends on its neighbors, turning swimming together into a game. To study this, we optimize the shape changes of soft swimmers, alone and in pairs, with a differentiable Stokes solver. From random initial membrane motions, a lone swimmer converges to a traveling membrane wave. In a pair, the stroke of a swimmer affects its neighbor far more than the neighbor affects its own best stroke. For swimmers in line, this influence decays as $1/\ell$ with their separation $\ell$, whereas the incentive to respond decays as $1/\ell^2$. Selfish swimmers, which maximize their own payoff, respond only to the weak incentive. The cooperative gain they miss decays only as $1/\ell^2$, and their selfish adaptations leave the pair worse off than if both had kept their solitary strokes. Related swimmers, which also value the payoff of their neighbor, recover this gain, whereas competitors pay to hinder each other, both following a law that we derive analytically. Hydrodynamics alone thus makes swimming in company a social dilemma, whose outcome depends on how much the swimmers value each other.

title: On Universal Minkowski Classes of Polytopes: Theory and Applications
abstract: This paper establishes the existence, in every dimension, of universal Minkowski classes of configuration-constrained polytopes, with direct applications to set-theoretic control. For any prescribed accuracy, such a class contains an approximation of every compact convex set to that accuracy and admits a jointly affine parameterization of facets and vertices. The construction is explicit and relies on a combinatorial averaging procedure that produces minimal configuration enclosures. In control, these polytopic templates enable convex reformulations of otherwise non-convex problems, including invariant-set computation and control Lyapunov function design. Tutorial examples illustrate both the geometric construction and its control applications.

title: A Robust High-order Approximation of the Gray Thermal Radiative Transfer Equations
abstract: We present a high-order, positivity preserving, and asymptotic preserving approximation of the gray radiative transfer equations. The time and space approximation is done using a diagonally-implicit Runge-Kutta method with stabilized, continuous finite elements, and the angular approximation uses the method of discrete ordinates. We detail a simple and robust inner/outer iteration strategy to solve these equations and prove that the proposed scheme is exactly conservative, independent of iterative tolerances. A maximum and minimum principle is enforced using a conservative redistribution limiting technique, and the method is demonstrated to be robust in the thick diffusion limit.

title: Prune Gradually, Adapt Sparsely: Efficient Pruning of Large Language Models at Extreme Sparsity
abstract: Weight pruning can reduce the storage and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but preserving quality at high sparsity levels remains challenging. Existing methods face a quality-cost trade-off in this regime. One-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply as sparsity increases, even when followed by post-pruning recovery. A growing line of work instead optimizes the mask directly from the dense model under the end-to-end objective; among these methods, [Lee et al.,2026], the recent state of the art at extreme sparsity, reaches high quality but at the cost of model-sized optimizer state and auxiliary variables. To address this gap, we propose ETAPS, which prunes gradually and adapts sparsely: it tightens a global sparsity constraint in progressive stages while training a sparse delta with a small, fixed budget. Our key observation is that gradual weight removal keeps each pruning step small enough for sparse adaptation to compensate, allowing the adapted model to provide end-to-end gradients that guide the next pruning decision without model-sized optimizer state. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, ETAPS achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity from 50% to 90%, with perplexity reductions of up to 42%. ETAPS is also far cheaper: at 90% sparsity, it prunes LLaMA2-7B on a single H200, where ELSA uses four, with $5.0\times$ smaller total persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours. Together, our findings point to a promising direction for achieving high quality in demanding regimes such as extreme sparsity at substantially lower cost.

title: Tensor cluster expansion as an efficient surrogate for multi-ACE
abstract: In this work, we generalize an on-lattice tensor cluster expansion (TCE) framework to an arbitrary correlation order. We show that these generalized tensor cluster expansion features span a subspace of MACE features, suggesting that TCE features can sufficiently pre-screen MACE features for chemical diversity in alloyed transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers. We show that, using maximum-entropy subset sampling, we can empirically recover chemical diversity from MACE features using a cheaper TCE representation. We then fine-tune a multi-ACE (MACE) potential with both subsets, and use this potential to predict temperature-dependent vibrational properties in alloyed TMD monolayers with varying chemical ordering. In our approach, TCE features can be used as cheap surrogate features for pre-screening chemically rich configurations using MACE features, allowing for the more efficient finetuning of atomic cluster expansion (ACE) potentials, thus achieving a tractable prediction of finite-temperature alloy thermodynamics on modest hardware.

title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
abstract: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.

title: The 3-Color 2-Chromatic Gallai-Ramsey Number for Complete Graphs
abstract: For $1\le i\le j\le k$, let $gr^3_2(K_i, K_j, K_k)$ be the least $n\in \mathbb{N}$ such that every rainbow triangle-free $3$-coloring of $K_n$ (using red, blue, and green) contains a red/blue $K_i$, a red/green $K_j$, or a blue/green $K_k$. In this paper, we completely evaluate $gr^3_2(K_i, K_j, K_k)$ for all values of $i$, $j$, and $k$ in which $r(K_i,K_j)$ is known.

title: Scattering of massless scalar waves by higher-dimensional regular black holes in general relativity coupled to nonlinear electrodynamics
abstract: We study the scattering of planar massless scalar waves by the family of higher-dimensional regular black holes in general relativity coupled to nonlinear electrodynamics, which unifies the Bardeen and Hayward models in any dimension. The scalar field is a neutral test field that propagates in the bulk, and in the geometric-optics limit, its rays are the null geodesics of the spacetime, so that the unstable circular null geodesics of the background geometry control the scattering. We combine the classical scattering of null geodesics, the glory approximation, which we generalize to $D$ dimensions, and the partial-wave analysis in $D=5,6,7$. We show that at a fixed frequency, the wave cross section diverges in the forward direction as $θ^{-4}$ in any dimension, with a coefficient fixed by the mass, while the steeper classical law $θ^{-(D-2)^{2}/(D-3)}$ appears only at larger angles and higher frequencies. The charge parameter decreases the critical and the glory impact parameters and widens the glory fringes, and in higher dimensions, the glory pattern has fewer and wider fringes and a weaker backward intensity. For the matched configurations studied here, backward intensity and low-frequency absorption provide the clearest differences, while the intermediate-to-high-frequency spectra are close.

title: Limit theorems for cuspidal orbits on Fuchsian groups
abstract: Let $Γ\subset \operatorname{SL}(2, \mathbb{R})$ be discrete, co-finite with cusps, and let ${\frak b}\in \mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$ be a cusp of $Γ$. Let $f: Γ{\frak b} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a quantum modular form in the sense that the maps $$ ϕ_γ(x) = f(x) - f(γx) \qquad (x\in Γ{\frak b}, γ\in Γ) $$ extend to Hölder-regular functions. Under bounded moments assumptions of the shape $\sum_n n^{-2} \int |ϕ_{γ^n}(x)|^αd x < \infty$ for some $α>0$ and every fixed parabolic element $γ\in Γ$, we prove asymptotic formulas for the characteristic functions of the values $f(x)$ for $x\in Γ{\frak b}$, ordered by growing denominators. These yield Gaussian limits when $α>2$ and other stable limit laws under suitable further assumptions. This generalizes to Fuchsian groups the work of Baladi-Vallée on rational orbits of the Gauss map. In companion papers, we use this result, and in particular its flexible assumptions on $ϕ_γ$, to deduce limit theorems for automorphic $L$-series at the central point. One ingredient in our proof is a particular cuspidal acceleration of the Bowen-Series map, whose inverse branches admit a convenient parametrization, and for which we describe explicitly a natural extension.

title: Model Checking for Metric Extensions of Monadic Second-Order Logic
abstract: Monadic second-order logic yields powerful algorithmic meta-theorems, but cannot express that a vertex set induces a shortest path. We study metric extensions of counting monadic second-order logic and identify structural parameters supporting efficient model checking, optimization, and counting. We show that shortest paths and equidistance guarded by geodesic cycles are definable in ordinary vertex-set MSO on graph classes of bounded cycle-basis length. This yields fixed-parameter tractable model checking for the corresponding extensions of CMSO2, parameterized by formula length and bag-connected treewidth, and of CMSO1, parameterized by formula length and geodesic cliquewidth: the sum of cliquewidth and cycle-basis length. The translations preserve free variables, yielding additive optimization and counting. Applications include Minimum Geodetic Set and Strong Metric Dimension for geodesic cliquewidth, and Minimum Isometric Path Partition for bag-connected treewidth. We also introduce restricted packing-covering templates that allow numerical distance thresholds to remain outside the parameter. For each fixed template, feasibility, additive vertex-weight optimization, and counting are fixed-parameter tractable in bag-connected treewidth. Applications include Distance-r Dominating Set, d-Scattered Set, and Minimum Eccentricity Shortest Path. Finally, we characterize bounded bag-connected treewidth and bounded geodesic cliquewidth through monadic dependence for the corresponding guarded logics. Unguarded distance comparisons have stricter structural boundaries: first-order model checking is AW[*]-complete already on uncolored caterpillars, and model checking a fixed existential monadic sentence is NP-complete on this class.

title: Novel Mixed Approximate Deconvolution Large-Eddy Simulation Models for Two-Phase Flows
abstract: Approximate Deconvolution (AD) frameworks for Large-Eddy Simulation (LES) offer a promising approach for modeling multiscale interactions in turbulent multiphase flows. However, some conventional formulations exhibit structural inconsistencies, identified in our previous work [Amani E., Molaei M.B., Ghorbani M. 2024 Novel mixed approximate deconvolution subgrid-scale models for large-eddy simulation. Physics of Fluids 36] which can impact the accuracy and robustness of AD-LES. To address this issue, the present study extends a family of structurally consistent AD closures to turbulent two-phase flows. Specifically, we introduce the Alternative Local Dynamic Model with Kinetic energy equation (A-LDMK), an improved non-equilibrium one-equation mixed eddy-viscosity AD framework. These closures are evaluated through a posteriori analyses of a single-phase turbulent channel flow and a turbulent two-phase gas-liquid mixing layer. The results indicate that the consistent frameworks enhance numerical stability and can sustain energy backscatter under less restrictive stability constraints compared to standard dynamic procedures. Specifically, the proposed A-LDMK provides the most accurate prediction of the multiscale primary atomization cascade in terms of droplet size distribution, compared to the other assessed closures.

title: Solvable coupled cluster states in $d=\infty$ with prescribed momentum distribution
abstract: Two of the most successful ideas in many-body theory, the exponential coupled cluster ansatz and DMFT, have to date developed separately. We establish a connection between them, by showing that the infinite dimensional limit of the hypercubic lattice allows the exact closed-form evaluation of static expectation values of coupled cluster wave functions, provided the cluster amplitudes admit a low-rank decomposition. As a result, evaluation errors -- a serious concern in conventional coupled cluster theory -- can be disentangled from limitations to expressivity of coupled cluster states. For this family of coupled cluster states, the cavity construction in $d\to\infty$ exactly reduces the environment of a lattice site to a Gaussian Grassmann kernel, and irreducible diagrams for one-body expectation values are found to be site-diagonal (in analogy to the DMFT self-energy). The resulting ``impurity problem" is an integral over a finite number of Grassmann variables rather than a dynamical quantum impurity problem, so that static observables derive exactly from a static self-consistency condition: a wave function counterpart of DMFT. For the simplest case of a cluster amplitude restricted to rank-one doubles, we obtain the momentum distribution in closed form. We show that any momentum distribution can be realized by a state that is the exact and unique ground state of an explicit parent Hamiltonian with a gapless single-particle tunnelling spectrum. By construction these coupled cluster states variationally recover low order perturbation theory for the Hubbard model. Their failure in the strong coupling regime near the Mott transition diagnoses a fundamental limitation of coupled cluster doubles. Intriguingly, our family of coupled cluster wave functions includes a gapless state with zero quasiparticle weight, with a momentum distribution that is completely smooth at the Fermi energy.

title: Hedetniemi's conjecture for Shannon OR-capacity: counterexamples and asymptotic separation
abstract: We disprove the analogue of Hedetniemi's conjecture for Shannon OR-capacity, which asserts that the capacity of a categorical product equals the smaller capacity of its factors. For every sufficiently large complete graph, we construct a second graph of larger capacity such that their categorical product has capacity strictly below that of the complete graph. Further constructions show that, for every real threshold above an explicit constant, both factor capacities can exceed that threshold while the product capacity lies below it. We also construct graph pairs, again with one complete factor, whose capacities tend to infinity while their product capacity is subpolynomial in the smaller factor capacity. Whether the product capacity must nevertheless tend to infinity whenever both factor capacities do remains open. The proofs use spectral interpolation, which also yields a single spectral point violating Hedetniemi's identity throughout the complete-factor family. Finally, we identify the categorical product as the distinguishability graph of a random-switching model for zero-error communication. In this model, our constructions show that switching can reduce the zero-error rate to a vanishing fraction of the smaller individual rate.

title: Language-Conditioned Behavioral Cloning for Autonomous Endoscope Guidance
abstract: Automated endoscope guidance reduces the need for continuous manual camera control during minimally invasive surgery. However, the desired camera motion depends on the surgeon's immediate intentions and cannot always be inferred from the visual operative scene alone. We propose to automate the task using language-conditioned behavioral cloning; we define 6 clinically relevant guidance behaviors and collect 235 subtask demonstrations. In preliminary phantom experiments, our policy achieves 100% success on focus, overview, and stop, 80% on search-tip and follow-tip behaviors, and 50% on horizon leveling. These results demonstrate the feasibility of learning heterogeneous surgeon-requested camera behaviors with a single visuomotor policy, while the observed failure modes motivate future work on adding temporal context for more demanding guidance tasks.

title: Combinatorial Calculations of the Most Probable Short-term Return of Single Company Stocks on the Stock Market
abstract: The combinatorial method is used to calculate the quantity of distribution variants for the number of stockholders of one individual company as well as the quantity of stocks in the stockholder portfolio. These quantities may change as a result of the stocks buy and sale that is taken into account also. The total number of stocks the units at the lower level of the problem is obviously preserved, while the number of portfolios - the structural units at the upper level may change. The most probable distributions of the number of portfolios and stocks in each of them are determined depending on the expense to add a stock to the portfolio (the purchase price). The application of the developed method to determine the most probable short term return on stocks in a combinatorial sense is demonstrated.

title: New Lower Bounds for Private PAC Learning
abstract: We study realizable PAC learning under approximate differential privacy, and give a framework for proving lower bounds on its sample complexity. We construct classes with identical VC and Littlestone dimensions but different private sample complexities at common privacy and accuracy parameters, showing that these dimensions do not determine the sample complexity, even for improper learners. To address this we introduce the Independent Class Packing (ICP) parameter, the largest total sample complexity of classes in $\mathcal{G}$ that can be packed independently into a class $\mathcal{H}$, and prove that every $(\varepsilon, δ)$-DP, $(α, β)$-PAC learner for $\mathcal{H}$, possibly improper, uses $Ω\left(\mathrm{ICP}(\mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G})/(α\varepsilon)\right)$ examples. Using this framework we prove tight lower bounds for axis-aligned rectangles, union of intervals and linear subspaces and improved lower bounds for halfspaces and convex polygons. Finally we also show that for product classes, and more generally when the same classes pack into $\mathcal{H}$ and cover its domain so that target labels can be used directly, ICP characterizes private PAC sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

title: Design and Validation of a Robotic Knee Exoskeleton with Musculoskeletal Simulation-Derived Biological Torque Control
abstract: Data-driven controllers have enabled lower-limb robotic exoskeletons to adapt assistance to the user across many tasks.
