A leading example is biological torque control, which estimates the user's own joint moment from onboard sensors and assists in proportion to that estimate. However, its estimators are trained on data recorded with the target device, so deploying the controller on new hardware requires collecting new data. Existing open-source efforts release hardware, software, or controllers separately, so this data collection must still be repeated on the assembled device. Here, we present an open-source knee exoskeleton, built from off-the-shelf components and widely available fabrication tools, with a biological torque controller derived entirely from simulation. A muscle-driven imitation policy reproduces squatting motions from an open biomechanics dataset, and the resulting knee moments are distilled into an estimator that uses only onboard sensors, so no training data are recorded on the device. In seven able-bodied participants, assistance reduced peak biological knee extension moment by 21.5% and peak vastus medialis activation by 26.7% during squatting, relative to squatting without the exoskeleton (p<0.05). Our results demonstrate that a biological torque controller derived from simulation can transfer to physical hardware without device-specific data collection. Because the hardware and training pipeline are released together, research groups can train and compare knee exoskeleton controllers on shared hardware without additional data collection overhead.

title: Suspended-Fabric Robotic Manipulation Surfaces: Modelling, Design Space, and Multimodular Extensio
abstract: Robotic Manipulation Surfaces (RMS) reposition objects by deforming the surface on which they rest. A recent class of RMS suspends a continuous fabric sheet from a sparse grid of vertical linear actuators lowering the actuator density of such surfaces but how to design such surfaces so that objects can be controlled everywhere on it, and how to extend it beyond a single module so that objects can pass between modules and achieve parallel, remain open. This paper presents a separable catenary model of the suspended sheet that is fast to compute and provides both the surface shape for given actuator heights and the actuator heights for a desired local slope. The closed form inverse lets a simple PID controller position objects on the sheet, and the model relates fabric length, module span and actuator stroke to the reachable workspace, yielding a minimum fabric length bound and design charts for these surfaces. The approach is then extended to a multimodular platform in which neighbouring modules share actuators. On a $2 \times 2$ prototype, we demonstrate that centimetre-scale objects are transferred between modules and positioned within 0.03 m over a $1 m^2$ workspace with only nine actuators, enabling multi-object manipulation and opening the way to parallel manipulation.

title: TwinPast: Benchmarking Historical Evidence Use in Streaming Video Understanding with Evidence Contrastive Video Pairs
abstract: High accuracy on streaming video benchmarks does not establish whether a model uses visual history. Our review of OVO-Bench and StreamingBench finds that recent frames suffice for 32% of sampled historical questions, while models also answer many questions correctly from the question and options alone. We introduce TwinPast to test whether answers correctly follow changes in history, using 350 human-reviewed video pairs spanning five historical tasks. Each pair holds the recent video context, question, and ordered options fixed while changing critical historical evidence and the correct answer. Each video is evaluated independently, and PairAcc requires correct answers for both histories. We evaluate 34 model and input configurations. For Qwen3-VL-8B and DeepSeek-Flash, historical inputs improve performance on TwinPast, reversing the recent-frame advantage on existing benchmarks. The strongest evaluated streaming system reaches 49.14% PairAcc, compared with 66.57-91.43% for the evaluated general-purpose models. This gap persists across all five tasks. Case studies further show that models select states from the wrong time or contradict recorded event order despite retaining the relevant evidence. These findings highlight the need to connect historical memory and retrieval with reasoning that uses evidence according to the question's temporal references and event relations.

title: Hilton-Zhao vertex-splitting conjecture for triangle-free graphs
abstract: Every graph obtained from a regular Class $1$ graph by a vertex-splitting is overfull and hence is of Class $2$; the central question is whether the resulting graph is edge-chromatic critical. We consider a revised version of the Hilton-Zhao vertex-splitting conjecture for triangle-free base graphs, excluding the known cubic exception that arises from the Wagner graph. Let $G$ be a connected $n$-vertex triangle-free $Δ$-regular Class $1$ graph, and let $G^{*}$ be obtained from $G$ by splitting one vertex into two adjacent vertices. We first show that any non-extreme vertex-splitting produces a $Δ$-critical graph provided $Δ>\frac{n-1}{3}$. Consequently, for non-extreme vertex-splittings, the revised version of the conjecture is valid across its entire conjectured degree range, and indeed even under a slightly weaker degree condition. We next turn to arbitrary vertex-splittings, extreme ones included. It is shown that $G^*$ is $Δ$-critical provided $n \ge 10$ and $Δ>\frac{2n-3}{5}$. In addition, for $n>24$, the non-strict condition $Δ\ge \frac{2n-3}{5}$ is already sufficient. This extends the bipartite range $Δ>\frac{2n}{5}$ to the boundary range that the bipartite argument does not cover. In particular, our arguments give a complete treatment of the case of triangle-free $6$-regular base graphs in the conjectured range. The proofs bring together structural properties of full-deficiency pairs, homomorphism theorems for dense triangle-free graphs, and Hamilton decompositions built via graph detachment.

title: Suspense and surprise in matroid bingo
abstract: We present the game of Matroid Bingo and prove that it gets more suspenseful the longer the game goes on.

title: Resource efficient Sample Based Quantum Simulation through Fragmentation and Virtual Partitioning of QPU
abstract: Present-day sample-based quantum algorithms within quantum-centric supercomputing workflows require substantial classical post-processing, large circuit depths to produce chemically relevant samples, and long QPU times to execute the many circuits needed for molecules of chemically relevant size. We introduce FMO-QVM-HCI-HSQD, a resource-efficient sample-based framework that breaks a large problem into fragments, runs the fragments in parallel on virtual regions of the QPU, and reduces circuit depth through a half-qubit ansatz whose samples seed an HCI expansion. We demonstrate the algorithm on ibm_marrakesh and ibm_boston for the water trimer and the carmofur_Mpro complex with up to 52 qubits, benchmarking against FMO-CCSD(T), FMO-CASCI and FMO-HCI. For the water trimer (14 spin orbitals for monomers, 28 for dimers), our method reduces the two-qubit depth by 39% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD and the QPU time by 82% compared to sequential FMO-SQD, and accesses 3% of the determinant subspace versus 40% for FMO-SQD, while achieving more accurate energies. For the carmofur_Mpro complex (16 and 32 spin orbitals), it reduces the two-qubit depth by 47% and the QPU time by 20% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD, and accesses 0.007% of the determinant subspace versus 40%, while remaining within chemical accuracy. Extending the carmofur_Mpro active space in the 6-31G basis to 52 and 104 spin orbitals, sampled on 26 and 52 qubits, the total energy deviates from FMO-HCI by only 1.22 mHa. These results show that combining fragmentation, virtual QPU partitioning and half-qubit sampling makes sample-based quantum simulation of chemically relevant systems feasible on current hardware.

title: FoAViS: Analyzing Learned Fixation Strategies in a Foveated Active Vision System
abstract: Human vision is foveated and active: resolution is highest at the fovea and falls off towards the periphery, and fixations are actively directed to locations of interest. Building a machine system that processes information in the same way lets us study gaze behavior in a controlled setting where the system's components and objectives are known. The emergence of gaze characteristics can therefore be examined systematically, which may in turn inform our understanding of biological vision. This requires a model that can sample like the fovea, handle various tasks from classification to dense prediction, and be trained concurrently with a fixation policy. In our study, we present such a system and study its capabilities and the fixation policies that emerge from it. Our system, FoAViS, samples visual input by adopting the established log-polar foveation and accumulates information in a 2D spatial memory. Due to its 2D structure, the same memory can be read out globally for classification or densely for semantic segmentation, without any architectural change. Fixations are drawn from a 2D map by a policy trained concurrently with the task. We find that learned fixation policies select more informative, task-specific locations than non-learned heuristics. These policies also shape the task representations in a beneficial way: for both classification and segmentation, models trained concurrently with a policy outperform models trained with random locations, even when the latter are provided with learned scanpaths. Moreover, these scanpaths exhibit similarities to human gaze behavior by capturing aspects of empirical scanpath characteristics. Our work marks an important step away from standard passive, single-pass architectures, towards biologically grounded models of vision. It opens a path for studying goal-directed gaze behavior and information representation in the visual system.

title: ID2Pattern: Pretraining Generalizable Identity Behavior Patterns for Transaction Risk Foundation Models
abstract: Large-scale behavioral pretraining offers a promising route to generalizable representations in online payment systems. However, high-cardinality identity fields such as card, device, and account IDs, though rich in behavioral signals, remain underexploited. Their continually growing vocabularies and limited semantic meaning make existing vocabulary-based and semantics-based encodings ill-suited. Their generalizable signal lies not in specific values, but in the identity behavior patterns they exhibit across a transaction sequence. Building on this insight, we propose ID2Pattern, a pretraining framework that brings these patterns into transaction foundation models. ID2Pattern first encodes identity fields with a Local Anonymous ID (LAID) tokenizer, which captures how each identity appears and recurs within the sequence, independent of its specific value. It then pretrains a multi-scale pattern codebook on unlabeled sequences, which abstracts LAID sequences into discrete behavior patterns for downstream prediction. Experiments on an industrial dataset with over 100M sequences and six public datasets show that ID2Pattern consistently outperforms strong baselines, improving industrial by 4.13% and public datasets by 8.83% on average. Notably, ID2Pattern remains equally effective even when all identity values are unseen during training, highlighting its potential to generalize to new users and markets.

title: Maximum of the Two-Dimensional Directed Polymer in the Critical Window
abstract: Let $Z_N^{β_N}(x)$ denote the partition function of the two-dimensional directed polymer started at $x\in \mathbb{Z}^2$, in Gaussian environemnt, in the critical window, with parameter $β_N=\sqrt{(1-\vartheta/\log N)/R_N}$. Here $R_N\sim (\log N)/π$ is the truncated collision Green function at the origin for the simple random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^2$. Let $\mathfrak M_N$ denote the maximum of $\log Z_N(x)$ over $|x|_\infty\leq \sqrt{N}$. We prove that, for any $\vartheta\in \mathbb{R}$, in probability, $$\mathfrak M_N/\sqrt{\log N}\to 2\sqrt{2}\text{ as }N\to\infty.$$

title: When is the deepest drawdown also the longest?
abstract: Does the deepest drawdown take the longest to recover? For random walks with iid increments of positive finite mean, we find that the deepest and longest episodes are eventually distinct almost surely under light-tailed losses, but coincide with probability tending to one under heavy-tailed losses. More precisely, when losses have a finite exponential moment, the deepest episode's duration, relative to the longest among $n$ episodes, converges in probability to an explicit $ρ\in(0,1)$, while its descending duration rank is $n^{1-ρ+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)}$. These limits hold for every fixed number of leading depths; in the Gaussian model, $ρ=1/2$, independently of drift and variance. The separation reflects the different exponential costs of reaching a large depth and sustaining a long episode. For regularly varying losses, a common large loss governs both depth and duration: the duration ratio tends to one almost surely, and for every fixed $k$, the $k$ deepest and $k$ longest episodes have the same indices in the same order with probability tending to one. For any $k_n\to\infty$ with $k_n=o(n)$, the proportion of common episodes among the $k_n$ deepest and $k_n$ longest converges in probability to zero in the light-tailed case and to one in the heavy-tailed case. These ranking laws also hold for completed drawdowns within a deterministic observation horizon.

title: Relaxation speed in quenched-random force fields
abstract: Disorder is commonly expected to slow down relaxation, as in glasses and disordered magnets. Here we show that this need not be the case in general, by analysing the asymptotic relaxation rate of a Brownian particle in a harmonic background potential and a quenched-random Gaussian force field with conservative and non-conservative components. Combining weak-disorder perturbation theory, random-matrix theory, and numerical solutions of the Fokker-Planck equation, we show that the outcome depends on the geometry of the background and on the properties of the random forces. We identify two distinct mechanisms that shape the relaxation speed: an effective stiffening of the background by the disorder, as previously reported in one dimension, and interactions (repulsive and attractive) between the levels of the Fokker-Planck operator. Through level attraction, a common feature of non-Hermitian operators, non-conservative driving forces pull the slowest mode towards faster ones, which facilitates faster relaxation. In anisotropic backgrounds, both effects occur at second order in the disorder strength, enabling either slower or faster relaxation. In isotropic backgrounds, level interactions dominate and the disorder affects the degenerate slowest mode already at first order. The shift is then given by the left-most eigenvalue of a Gaussian random matrix and relaxation is generically slowed down. In backgrounds whose anisotropy is comparable to the disorder strength, level attraction is most effective by merging the slowest mode with its neighbour into an oscillating complex-conjugate pair. In this case, relaxation becomes faster on average once the random forces are sufficiently non-conservative. Our results draw a nuanced picture of how disorder affects the asymptotic relaxation speed in complex systems and uncover general mechanisms that are likely to apply beyond the current setting.

title: MoETok: Sparse Expert Routing for 1D Visual Tokenizers
abstract: Modern visual tokenizers aim to preserve fine-grained visual details while learning high-level semantic representations for downstream generation and understanding. Query-based 1D visual tokenizers encode images into flexible latent sequences, yet how individual learnable queries gather and encode image information remains poorly understood. We reveal that these queries spontaneously develop complementary roles under semantic supervision: a small set of Content queries captures high-level semantic information, while a larger set of Detail queries preserves fine-grained visual details for reconstruction. To adapt token processing to these heterogeneous roles, we introduce MoETok, a 1D visual tokenizer that routes tokens through sparsely activated experts. Jointly optimized with reconstruction and semantic objectives, the router learns role-specialized processing paths adapted to each token's representation. Across model scales and token budgets, MoETok consistently improves reconstruction, semantic representation, and autoregressive generation over dense tokenizers under matched supervision and active computation. On ImageNet, it combines strong reconstruction and semantic representation with state-of-the-art class-conditional generation within the 1D tokenizer family. We further validate MoETok at scale in a unified autoregressive model jointly trained for understanding and generation with a next-token cross-entropy objective. The resulting model combines competitive visual understanding with state-of-the-art generation among unified discrete models, matching or surpassing diffusion-based models such as BAGEL and Qwen-Image on benchmarks including DPG-Bench (87.61), GenEval2 (40.04 GM), and WISE (0.49).

title: Large-Time Upper Decay Estimates for Weakly Coupled Time-Fractional Diffusion Systems
abstract: We prove conjectured-optimal large-time upper decay estimates for solutions of weakly coupled systems of $m\ge2$ time-fractional diffusion equations. Our result establishes the upper-bound assertion in the conjecture of Li, Liu, and Wada~\cite{LLW26}. The sharpness of these upper exponents for $m\ge3$ remains open in general; see Section~\ref{sec:discussion}. Assume that the diffusion matrices are uniformly elliptic, the coupling coefficients are bounded and may depend on time, and the matrix of $L^\infty$-norms of the coupling coefficients satisfies a spectral-radius stability condition. Let $α^*$ denote the smallest fractional order among the components with nonzero initial data. Then the $L^2(Ω)^m$-norm of the solution is $O(t^{-α^*})$ as $t\to\infty$ if $α^*<1$, whereas it is $O(t^{-(1+α_m)})$ if $α^*=1$, where $α_m$ is the smallest fractional order occurring in the system. For $m=2$, the result yields the same upper decay exponents as \cite[Theorem~1.1]{LLW26}; in the absence of self-coupling, the matrix stability condition is weaker than the corresponding small-coupling condition in that work. The case $m\ge3$ is new. Our proof uses a large-time weighted Volterra framework. If $α^*<1$, the weight is a regularly varying power weight; if $α^*=1$, it is constructed by convolution with the resolvent kernel associated with the smallest fractional order. These weights yield the required large-time bounds for all resolvent kernels in the system. In particular, the argument avoids the Laplace-transform and residue-calculus methods used in \cite{LLW26}, which become difficult to implement for systems with three or more components.

title: DAMI: Dual-Axis Memory Initialization for Enhanced Long-Context Retrieval in Gated Linear Attention
abstract: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.

title: On Statistical-Computational Gaps in Graph Combinatorial Testing Problems
abstract: We study high-dimensional graph combinatorial hypothesis testing problems in which a signal is supported on the edge set of an unknown subgraph drawn from a class invariant under vertex relabeling. For Gaussian observations, we characterize sharp statistical and computational thresholds (at polynomial order) for the signal magnitude required for strong detection across various combinatorial graph alternatives. Our analysis is based on bounding the second moments of the full and low-degree likelihood ratios in terms of the overlap of two independent latent structures and comparing the resulting lower bounds with scan, average, and coordinatewise maximum tests. Under an appropriate low-degree conjecture for computational hardness, we obtain planted-clique thresholds matching those known for Gaussian submatrix detection and identify new statistical-computational gaps for multiple planted cliques and hypercliques, thick cycles and thick paths. We also establish a novel transfer principle across natural exponential family observation models: matching the one-coordinate chi-square divergence preserves full likelihood-ratio second moments exactly and makes low-degree second moments equivalent up to constant factors under a degree condition. Under local regularity, we obtain corresponding testing upper bounds in terms of an effective signal strength. When these upper and lower bounds match, they yield universal threshold scales in the local alternative regime. As a consequence, statistical-computational gaps for planted-clique detection in Erdős--Rényi settings can be deduced from the Gaussian model.

title: Rationally slice knots that are not biprojectively H-slice
abstract: We show that rationally slice knots need not be biprojectively H-slice (BPH-slice), answering a question in the study of the rational knot concordance group. Our main tool is a lattice embedding obstruction to H-sliceness in $\#^n\mathbb{CP}^2$ for knots with vanishing signature, extending work of Kjuchukova--Miller--Ray--Sakallı. We apply the obstruction to an infinite family of rationally slice knots, beginning with $8_{18}$. As additional applications, we obstruct the BPH-sliceness of a family of 2-bridge knots which is not obstructed by the instanton knot concordance invariant $r_0$, we obstruct a non-alternating family of Montesinos knots, and we give prime alternating knots that are topologically but not smoothly biprojectively H-slice. We discuss why these knots remain plausible candidates for detecting exotic smooth structures on $\#^n\mathbb{CP}^2$ and suggest natural sources of further candidates.

title: Grid-Refinement SBL for AFDM Channel Estimation Under Fractional Delay and Fractional Doppler Channels
abstract: This paper investigates channel estimation for affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) systems over channels with fractional delay and fractional Doppler (FDFD) shifts. An exact FDFD channel model is first established, and the corresponding input--output relationship is also derived. To address the FDFD-induced delay--Doppler coupling, a first-order linear approximation grid-refinement sparse Bayesian learning (FLA-GR-SBL) method is developed. To further remedy the convergence and stability issues caused by the limited accuracy of the first-order approximation, we propose a two-dimensional grid-approximation SBL (2D-GA-SBL) algorithm, which iteratively refines the delay--Doppler grid and thereby characterizes the channel more accurately. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithms significantly outperform existing on-grid and off-grid SBL benchmarks in terms of both normalized mean square error (NMSE) and bit error rate (BER).

title: SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security
abstract: Recognized as a top threat to AI agents, prompt injection allows instructions from untrusted data (email, documents, websites) to manipulate the agent's operation. The existing best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign, is trained with the DPO loss but still suffers from attack success rates (ASRs) approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections. One reason is that DPO anchors the model around the undefended reference model, which is insecure. We show an idealized reference model---an injection-invariant, utility-preserving oracle---can nevertheless be approximated, as its output distribution in training is interestingly accessible. This new observation motivates a theoretically principled SecPO loss. Another Meta-SecAlign shortcoming is that it trains on weak simulated attacks. We implement an efficient adversarial training (AT) pipeline that synthesizes strong injected inputs (best@240), and train the model on them. Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5-14.5$\times$ across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4-4.6$\times$ compared with using DPO loss. In agentic workflows, our SecPO + AT Qwen3.6-27B is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the AttackerMovesSecond attack. Moreover, our defended model shows no noticeable reduction in benign utility in nine benchmarks covering agentic tool calling, instruction following, science, and math. We release our $\href{//github.com/Sizhe-Chen/SecPO}{\text{code}}$, $\href{//huggingface.co/datasets/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO-trainset}{\text{training data}}$ (with optimized injections from AT), and $\href{//huggingface.co/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO}{\text{model}}$.

title: Ramsey numbers $R(K_{1,4},K_{m,n})$ for small $m$
abstract: We determine all currently unknown values of the generalized two-color Ramsey number $R(K_{1,4},K_{m,n})$ for $\min(m,n) \leq 8$. We also prove that the number $R(K_{1,4},K_{m,m})$ equals $26, 29, 31, 33$ for $m = 9, 10, 11, 12$ respectively.

title: Less Loss, Fixed Weights: Logit Corrections for Forgetting
abstract: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final token predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a temperature. On text held out from correction fitting, the largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%, with loss conditional on the retained vocabulary. Combining the bias with a temperature recovers up to 36%. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of our restricted fits.

title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

title: GeoFlip: Benchmarking Geometry-Sensitive Physics in Video Generation
abstract: Video generation models synthesize realistic motion, but can they respond correctly to changes in initial geometry? We introduce GeoFlip, a video generation benchmark centered on physical outcome flips induced by geometry. With shared physical settings and textual prompts held fixed, GeoFlip applies controlled interventions to support extent, object placement, and mechanism configuration, constructing paired scenes with contrasting reference events, such as remaining stable versus falling or tipping. These pairs test whether models translate geometric differences in the first frame into correct physical evolution. The benchmark comprises 482 scene pairs and 964 reference videos across six physical categories, with reference outcomes established through procedural scene construction, physics simulation, and numerical validation and verification of physical events. We evaluate 16 models for image to video generation along three dimensions: event correctness, structural integrity, and similarity to reference videos. We examine evaluation consistency with independent vision language judges. On the 442 conditions shared by all models, the highest event correctness averaged across tasks is 27.98%, revealing substantial limitations in physical generation conditioned on geometry. Model strengths vary across physical mechanisms, and the three evaluation dimensions capture distinct capabilities. Typical failures include ignoring geometric changes, generating incorrect object motion, bending rigid objects, and introducing additional components. Rank correlations between judges reach 0.906 for event correctness and 0.929 for structural integrity. By combining controlled geometric interventions, verifiable physical references, and multidimensional evaluation, GeoFlip assesses progress from visual realism toward physical consistency conditioned on geometry.

title: Gearbox cavities: Ultrahigh wave confinement via broken rotational symmetry
abstract: Cavity enhancement of emission from a point source typically relies on structures that preserve its cylindrical symmetry, such as circular Bragg gratings. Combining inverse design with fundamental limits, we show that breaking this symmetry is necessary to maximize the local density of states in lossless two-dimensional cavities. Symmetry-broken designs exceed limits over all cylindrically symmetric structures by up to eight orders of magnitude, acting as ``gearboxes'' that convert the source's emission into high-angular-momentum waves trapped behind a centrifugal barrier.

title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents
abstract: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.

title: Tiling without a subspace complement: a sharp counterexample in dimension nine over the field with two elements
abstract: We construct an explicit 64-point subset of $\mathbb F_2^9$ which tiles by translation but has no linear-subspace tiling complement. Together with our earlier dimension-eight theorem and a product argument, this shows that every nonempty tile in $\mathbb F_2^d$ has a linear-subspace complement precisely when $d\le8$. The example is spectral, so it is not a counterexample to Fuglede's conjecture. Its construction uses six three-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb F_2^6$, specified by a small table. We classify all its tiling complements and spectra: there are exactly 512 complements and 64 spectra, with one translation class of each. Every spectrum has normalized Wiener norm $15/8$. An appendix proves that Goyal's related construction is affinely inequivalent but has the same tiling complements and spectra. The construction and both classifications are proved from first principles. We also give elementary proofs of the positive assertion in dimensions at most seven and for all tile sizes other than sixteen in dimension eight. The remaining case uses our previously established theorem based on the classification of perfect binary codes of length fifteen.

title: Extremal character spectra of finite projective systems
abstract: Let $\mathcal M$ be a finite spanning multiset of points in ${\rm PG}(k-1,q)$, and let ${\rm Char}_{\mathcal M}$ be its character function. For $1\le r\le k$, we study the maximum number of distinct values attained by ${\rm Char}_{\mathcal M}$ on the codimension-$r$ flats under a total-multiplicity budget. The spectrum is subject to two natural upper bounds, whose extremal cases lead respectively to $r$-maximum character spectrum ($r$-MCS) and $r$-full character spectrum ($r$-FCS) systems. We establish the existence of $r$-FCS systems in a broad parameter range, and solve the size-constrained extremal problem completely when $r=k-1$, including the minimum-cost multiplicity profiles. For $1\le r<k$, put $M_r=\qbinom{k}{r}$ and $B_r=\qbinom{k-1}{r}$. The minimum size $ν_r(k,q)$ of an $r$-MCS system satisfies \[\left\lceil\frac{\binom{M_r}{2}}{B_r}\right\rceil\le ν_r(k,q)\le \binom{M_r-1}{2}+\frac{q^k-q^{k-r}}{q-1}.\] The upper bound is at most $\binom{M_r}{2}$, strictly less when $r\le k-2$, and exact when $r=k-1$. Its proof applies positive additive labelings to the complement of one flat, whose trace is empty while all remaining traces are distinct. For $r=1$, we improve the known upper bounds on the minimum length of such systems. We also develop global moment identities and local flat-incidence bounds that impose strong structural constraints on large character spectra. Under the projective-system correspondence, complementary character spectra are the support-weight spectra of $r$-dimensional subcodes.

title: Anomalies of TQFTs coupled to parameter spaces and constraints on ground-state degeneracies
abstract: Anomalies of global symmetries can arise in long-range entangled quantum many-body systems and provide useful constraints on their dynamics. In this paper, we study anomalies of $d$-dimensional topological quantum field theories (TQFTs) coupled to parameter spaces and their implications for ground-state degeneracies. Specifically, we formulate anomalies as obstructions to constructing parametrized families of TQFTs. We discuss how the classification of these anomalies depends on the choice of topology on the universal $\mathrm{U}(1)$ $(d-1)$-form symmetry. In this framework, we use the projective ground-state bundle obtained by compactifying the TQFT on a spatial manifold to derive a general constraint relating its ground-state degeneracy $N$ to its torsion anomaly $ω$, expressed as $N\int_Wω\in\mathbb{Z}$ for bundles $W$ of spatial manifolds over closed surfaces. We apply this constraint to ground-state degeneracies of (2+1)-dimensional TQFTs with framing and 1-form symmetry anomalies and to obstructions to symmetry-preserving TQFTs. We also discuss implications for bordism generators and propose a conjecture on anomaly detection by manifolds fibered over surfaces.

title: Central values of additive twists of automorphic $L$-series
abstract: We study series $L(x,s):=\sum_n ρ(n)e^{2πi n x}/n^s$, where $ρ(n)$ are Fourier coefficients of an automorphic form $ϕ$ for a discrete cofinite subgroup $Γ\subset \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Let $\mathfrak{b}\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$ represent a cusp of $Γ$. Ordering the orbit $Γ\mathfrak{b}$ by increasing denominators, we prove that the values $L(x,1/2)$ for $x\inΓ\mathfrak{b}$, suitably normalized, become equidistributed according to a standard complex Gaussian law, under natural assumptions on the Laplace eigenvalue of $ϕ$. Previously this was known either when $Γ=\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ or when $ϕ$ is associated to a holomorphic cusp form. This applies in particular to central values at $s=1/2$ of additive twists of Maass form $L$-functions $\sum_{n\geq1}λ(n)e^{2πi n x}/n^s$, or to the Dirichlet-theta series $\sum_{n\geq1}χ(n)e^{2πi n^2 x}/n^s$.

title: An end-to-end CNN search for ultra-short-period planets in TESS: from the blend ceiling to the independent validation of TOI-6662 b
abstract: We trained a convolutional neural network to detect ultra-short-period planets in TESS photometry, following the procedure now standard in the field: synthetic transits as positives, eclipsing binaries as negatives. Measured that way it reaches an area under the ROC curve of 0.97. Keeping the same model and the same planets, but replacing the negatives with false positives that the TESS Follow-up Observing Program has actually rejected, the area falls to 0.50 -- the value of a random classifier. The conventional benchmark had been measuring a problem that does not exist. The reason is physical, and it bounds what is possible. Of 145 such false positives examined at pixel level, 42% are blends: eclipses belonging to a neighbouring star, diluted into the target aperture. Their light curves are indistinguishable from shallow transits, capping the attainable area at 1 - f/2 = 0.79. Retraining on real false positives reaches 0.80 +/- 0.06, confirming the ceiling independently. No classifier reading a single-band light curve can do better. A detector alone is the wrong instrument. We built CASCADE-USP, a pipeline chaining the network with difference-image centroid analysis, scene modelling with high-resolution imaging and the Gaia astrometric solution, supplying in sequence what the light curve lacks. Its output is a prioritisation, not a verdict: it records what evidence each candidate still needs. Only the classifier is domain-specific; the other stages apply to any transit candidate. Of 435 unresolved TESS candidates it isolates 20; 19 prove false positives, traced to causes invisible in TESS photometry. The twentieth is TOI-6662 b, an Earth-sized planet (0.94 +/- 0.03 Earth radii) orbiting an M dwarf every 7.05 hours. Our validation, independent of a concurrent one, agrees with it in planetary parameters and classification, closing the CASCADE procedure with an external check.

title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish
abstract: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. Its gain over a zero-shot Turkish language model is largest for speakers seen in training, while on unseen speakers it matches this strong baseline. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.

title: The C-3PO Framework: Algorithms for $\#\mathrm{BIS}$-Hard Problems on Graphs with Low Threshold Rank or High Girth
abstract: We give approximate counting and sampling algorithms for spin models on graphs of low threshold rank or high girth. Given any $n$-vertex graph $G$, let $k_η= k_η(G)$ count normalized-Laplacian eigenvalues strictly below $η$. For $\varepsilon > 0$, an $\varepsilon$-approximate counting algorithm outputs an estimate $\widehat Z$ of the partition function $Z$ satisfying $(1-\varepsilon)Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z$ with probability at least $3/4$. An $\varepsilon$-approximate sampling algorithm outputs a configuration whose distribution is within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the target distribution. We give the following results: (a) Ferromagnetic Potts. Fix $q\ge2$ and $η\in(0,1]$. There exists $β_0(q,η)$ such that, for every inverse temperature $β\geβ_0$, the zero-field $q$-state Potts model admits approximate counting and sampling algorithms: (i) On arbitrary graphs in time $\exp(O(k_η))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (ii) Fix $Δ\ge 3$. On $Δ$-regular graphs of girth $g$ in time $\exp(O(n e^{-g})) \operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (b) Bipartite hard-core. Fix $Δ\ge3$ and $η\in(0,1]$. There exists $λ_0(Δ,η)$ such that, for every fugacity $λ\geλ_0$, the hard-core model admits approximate counting and sampling: (i) On $Δ$-regular vertex-transitive bipartite graphs in time $\exp(O (k_η))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ (ii) On $Δ$-regular bipartite graphs of girth $g$ in $\exp(O(n e^{- g}))\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon).$ All four results follow from verifying the hypotheses of a new framework we call C-3PO. At a high level, the C-3PO algorithm proceeds by enumerating small cuts and reconstructing the original measure through cluster expansions. Underlying the algorithm is an improvement of subspace enumeration methods via active regression.

title: 3SUM Made Simpler (Without Matrix Multiplication), $k$-SUM Hypothesis Refuted for Odd $k$, and Real 3SUM/APSP Derandomized
abstract: Recently, a truly subquadratic algorithm for the 3SUM problem and a truly subcubic algorithm for the all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) problem were found by Anthropic, as reported by Alman and Vassilevska Williams (2026). These algorithms relied on a new subroutine for rectangular matrix multiplication with selected output entries, which was obtained by modifying known matrix multiplication techniques of Schönhage (1981) and Coppersmith (1982). 1. We present a different truly subquadratic randomized algorithm for 3SUM for integer inputs. It completely avoids the use of matrix multiplication but instead modifies known dynamic programming algorithms for subset convolution and the zeta transform, which rely only on simple subtraction tricks via inclusion--exclusion (and does not even require fast Fourier transform), and so is conceptually easier to understand (the whole solution is about 5 pages long). 2. Following a similar approach, we obtain a randomized algorithm for $k$-SUM for integer inputs for odd constant $k$ in $O(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil-\varepsilon_k})$ time for some constant $\varepsilon_k>0$, disproving the $k$-SUM Hypothesis for all odd $k$. 3. Existing reductions from 3SUM and APSP to selected-entries rectangular matrix multiplication were randomized in the case of real-valued input. We present new deterministic reductions, yielding a truly subquadratic deterministic algorithm for Real 3SUM and a truly subcubic deterministic algorithm for Real APSP.

title: When Does Jacobian Fine-Tuning Stabilize Neural PDE Emulators?
abstract: Neural emulators of chaotic PDEs are trained on one-step prediction but deployed autoregressively, where their errors compound. Jacobian-based regularisers aim to curb this growth, but in a chaotic system part of the growth is physical and cannot be trained away. We separate the two sources of this error with a first-order decomposition. We compare the emulator's error with a counterfactual that propagates the same one-step mistakes through the solver's Jacobian, giving an amplification ratio: the factor by which the model's own dynamics amplify its errors. We study 21 configurations across four PDEs, five architectures and two model sizes (8-10k and 33k parameters), with errors measured at one Lyapunov time. Jacobian fine-tuning reduced the error by more than 10% for 1 of 34 seeds whose amplification ratio was at most 1.25, and for all 20 seeds whose ratio was at least four; for the latter, the error fell by a factor of 8 (small models) and 55 (33k models) in geometric mean over seeds. The gain approximately equals the one-step accuracy cost of fine-tuning divided by the amplification ratio. Matching the solver's Jacobian along the model's own error direction (EDJM) outperformed random directions at the same cost on 28 of 35 seeds; input-noise injection performed comparably to EDJM.

title: Risk Assessment of Fair Multi-Period Dynamic Operating Envelopes under Uncertainty
abstract: Dynamic operating envelopes (DOEs) can allocate time-varying export capacity to distributed energy resources (DERs), and while they are not intended to make operations immune to voltage violations, they should guide operations to mostly remain inside expected values under changing regimes and residual forecast errors. However, although recent literature proposed many different techniques for implementing DOEs, there is sparse discussion of analyzing and quantifying the risk of using more or less conservative DOEs under uncertain operating regimes. Having this gap in mind, this paper develops a risk-oriented extension of a previously established fair distributed multi-period optimal power flow (OPF) framework, where fair or technical DOEs are fixed as first-stage decisions and the OPF leverages battery energy storage and renewable curtailment as recourse under regime uncertainties. An independent nonlinear AC power flow then computes a resulting ensemble, which is summarized by (i) voltage-violation probability, severity, and a persistence metric for consecutive out-of-band hours, (ii) curtailment and Jain and Gini indices, and (iii) model deviations. Different probability situations are assessed, ranging from uniform, sunny-heavy, night-peak-heavy, and adversarial, which separate the envelope design from the assumed operating distribution. An optional outer loop allows for fine-tuning a fairness--efficiency parameter under explicit violation and persistence budgets. The combination of the outer loop and the overall framework, which quantifies how often and how severely operating limits are exceeded, creates an auditable methodology mixing equitable export allocation, distributed recourse, and AC risk assessment for active distribution network operators, and this framework is assessed using up to 1000 Monte Carlo scenarios per mixture and DOE design.

title: Algebraic models of alpha-cluster nuclei
abstract: In this contribution I review the algebraic cluster model (ACM) for $α$-conjugate nuclei with $A=4n$ and its extension to the cluster shell model (CSM) for $A=4n+x$ nuclei. The CSM describes the splitting of single-particles levels in a deformed field generated by the cluster of $α$-particles. As an example, I discuss the energies, electromagnetic transitions and form factors of the neighboring nuclei $^{12}$C and $^{13}$C.

title: Physics-Informed Latent Neural ODEs for Reduced-Order Modeling of Hydrogen, Ammonia, and Methane Combustion Kinetics
abstract: Detailed chemical kinetic mechanisms are computationally expensive in reacting-flow simulations because of their high dimensionality and numerical stiffness. We develop an end-to-end physics-informed autoencoder neural ordinary differential equation (PI-AE-NODE) framework in which an encoder compresses the thermochemical state into a low-dimensional latent space, a Neural ODE advances it continuously in time, and a decoder reconstructs the temperature and all species mass fractions. Elemental conservation, mass conservation, and enthalpy consistency are embedded in the training objective. The framework is applied to H$_2$/air, NH$_3$/air, and CH$_4$/air autoignition using detailed mechanisms of increasing size and complexity, which are represented accurately with only a few latent variables. Compared with an otherwise identical data-driven model, the physical constraints improve ignition delay prediction and conservation behaviour. The models reproduce major and intermediate species evolution at both training and unseen conditions, and their latent dynamics permit efficient explicit integration, with the computational advantage over the detailed mechanisms increasing with mechanism size.

title: Logical Bell Inequalities for Marginal Wigner Negativity
abstract: We construct logical Bell inequalities whose violations are determined by the Wigner function of a reduced quantum state. For odd-prime qudits, each phase-space point of any nonempty proper subsystem defines an inequality, violated precisely when the corresponding Gross Wigner value is negative. This correspondence allows us to quantify the contextuality that a reduced state guarantees for the composite system. The normalized violation gives a lower bound on the contextual fraction in the complete Weyl measurement scenario, valid for every joint state with that marginal, irrespective of its correlations. We identify a family of product states that saturates this bound. For these states, one marginal Wigner value fixes the contextual fraction of the entire system.

title: Asynchronous Flow Map Language Models
abstract: The order in which tokens are predicted in language modeling has a profound impact on the quality of generated sequences. Autoregressive and masked diffusion models iteratively fill in tokens and can exploit such orderings across generation steps, but how to leverage an ordering for one-step parallel language modeling is unclear. We introduce asynchronous flow map language models (aFMLMs), which incorporate prediction order into one-step modeling by learning the flow maps of asynchronous flows. These flows specify an ordering through a tokenwise time schedule that controls the relative denoising progress of tokens. We formulate a general class of asynchronous flows that admit both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive schedules, show that they define valid flow maps, and develop new methods for their flow map distillation. The resulting models can generate all tokens in a single forward pass by internalizing the ordering encoded in the flow into their hidden computations. On Sudoku solving and code generation for GSM8K math word problems, aFMLM establishes new state-of-the-art one-step performance.

title: Modulo k-orientations of highly edge-connected signed graphs
abstract: A modulo $k$-orientation of a signed graph is an orientation in which the outdegree and indegree are congruent modulo $k$ at every vertex. We show that, for every odd integer $k\ge3$, every essentially $k$-unbalanced $(6k-10)$-edge-connected signed graph admits a modulo $k$-orientation. This improves the edge-connectivity bound of Zhu [JCTB, 112 (2015)] from $6k-7$ to $6k-10$.

title: Bootstrapping a Higher-Derivative Cosmological Collider: Borel-Laplace Resummation and Stokes Phenomena
abstract: We develop a higher-derivative cosmological bootstrap for massive spectators with quartic dispersion, $ω^2\propto k^4$, revealing a new boundary-value problem for inflationary correlators. The exchange equation becomes fourth order, and the collapsed limit becomes an irregular singular point, where collider and WKB branches coexist and exhibit Stokes phenomena. Since the folded configuration is now an ordinary point, the relativistic criterion of Bunch--Davies regularity at the folded singularity is no longer available. We instead impose an asymptotic boundary condition that removes the WKB branches and matches the surviving collider branches to Schwinger-Keldysh data. We also construct a convergent Borel-Laplace particular solution that resums a factorially divergent expansion and satisfies both bootstrap equations simultaneously; its leading collapsed-limit behavior is reproduced by direct in-in integrals. In the bispectrum, the squeezed-limit collider signal retains its mass-dependent frequency, while its amplitude and phase depend on the dispersion scale; near the equilateral configuration, the full shape is also sensitive to this scale and can change sign. Our results expose a new analytic structure of non-relativistic cosmological correlators and signatures beyond the squeezed limit.

title: Nexus-VLA: Bridging Human and Robot Experiences via a Shared Hierarchical Semantic Latent Space
abstract: Large-scale egocentric human videos provide rich and scalable manipulation experience for robot policy learning, yet substantial embodiment gaps in visual appearance, kinematic structure, and action spaces hinder effective knowledge transfer. Existing methods often decouple cross-embodiment knowledge alignment from robot policy learning, making it difficult for human manipulation knowledge to directly and fully contribute to robot action learning. To address this issue, we propose Nexus-VLA, a hybrid policy learning framework that enables cross-embodiment knowledge transfer through end-to-end human-robot joint training, allowing human manipulation experience to directly contribute to robot policy learning. We first introduce a hierarchical cross-embodiment semantic alignment paradigm that progressively establishes shared manipulation semantics from task intent to fine-grained interactions, enabling more complete use of the manipulation knowledge contained in human videos. Building on this hierarchy, we design a shared manipulation latent representation that jointly encodes multi-level shared knowledge into an internal representation directly used for continuous action generation, improving policy learning efficiency while effectively leveraging human knowledge. Across RoboCasa-GR1, OOD settings, and real-world robot experiments, Nexus-VLA achieves an 80.5% task success rate on RoboCasa-GR1 and demonstrates strong advantages in human-data utilization, learning efficiency, and cross-scenario generalization.

title: Spectral Beurling-Selberg Approximation and Applications to Effective Motivic Chebotarev-Sato-Tate Estimates
abstract: We establish a spectral Beurling-Selberg approximation theorem on compact connected Riemannian manifolds for sets whose boundaries have finite upper Minkowski content. Our majorants and minorants have controlled spectral coefficients and explicit stability under Hausdorff perturbations, uniformly over families satisfying a common Minkowski content bound. We extend the construction to singular spaces arising from Riemannian submetries with basic mean curvature, and apply it to equidistribution on quaternionic Shimura varieties. Assuming the conjectural formalism of the specified motivic L-functions, including the motivic Riemann hypothesis, we develop effective Chebotarev-Sato-Tate estimates for fixed sets and varying families with controlled boundary geometry and Hausdorff variation, and describe how additional symmetries improve the error exponents. The proofs combine classical analytic methods with new methods from differential geometry, analytic geometry, and Riemannian spectral analysis. Applications include an asymptotic formula for a motivic analogue of Atkin-Serre estimates and tubular estimates for Picard-rank jumps of K3 surfaces via their transcendental motives.

title: Capacity Meets the Four Subspace Problem: Distributed Linear Computation and the Cross-Ratio
abstract: $K$ users each observe a fixed linear function of common data over a finite field of characteristic $p$, and a server must recover another fixed linear function with zero error from one message sent by each user. The capacity, the minimum total number of symbols the users send per computed instance, depends only on the configuration of subspaces formed by these linear functions. We study the instance in which three users observe $\boldsymbol{a}$, $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{a}+\boldsymbol{b}$ and the server wants $\boldsymbol{a}+λ\boldsymbol{b}$. The four functions span four lines in a plane with cross-ratio $λ$, the smallest instance of the four subspace problem of representation theory. It is the smallest configuration whose capacity is not determined by the dimensions of the subspaces formed by sums and intersections: these dimensions are the same for every $λ$, but the capacity depends on the cross-ratio and on the prime subfield. For the harmonic cross-ratios, $λ=-1$, $λ=2$ or $2λ=1$, it is $2$: every zero-error code reveals $(\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b})$ to the server, so no code beats having two users send their observations. For $λ$ outside the prime subfield it is the cut-set bound $3/2$, achieved by codes linear over the prime subfield, while codes linear over the field need $2$. For the other $λ$ in the prime subfield it lies in $[3p/(2p-1),2]$, so no code at any block length approaches the cut-set bound. The qualitative separation persists under vanishing error for uniform data: the cut-set bound is tight exactly for $λ$ outside the prime subfield. The four-line instance is also exact repair of one node of a $[4,2]$ MDS storage code, and the results translate to that setting.

title: Know When the Equation Is Wrong: Structural Uncertainty for LLM-Guided Symbolic Regression under Extrapolation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can help discover mathematical equations from data, but most LLM-guided symbolic regression methods focus on a single best equation without quantifying uncertainty over alternative functional forms. This is challenging because distinct equations can fit the observed data similarly while producing substantially different extrapolations. Our experiments on the LLM-SRBench dataset show that standard conformal intervals achieve nominal in-distribution coverage but frequently fail under extrapolation. To tackle this challenge, we introduce LLM-SR-UQ, a framework that retains competing equation structures and uses their disagreement to characterize uncertainty about the underlying functional form. We extend the standard fixed-width conformal approach to quantify structural intervals, which measure disagreement among candidate equations and identify where prediction intervals should widen. Extensive experiments show our framework substantially improves coverage attainment by incorporating structural disagreement while preserving in-distribution coverage. Our approach also shows good generalizability when it is applied to other symbolic-regression methods.

title: Stochastic processes on reductive homogeneous and symmetric spaces
abstract: In this paper we present a method to effectively and efficiently provide pathwise approximations of the Riemannian Brownian motion on a reductive homogeneous space $M\cong G/H$ endowed with a $G$-invariant metric. This setting includes spheres, hyperbolic spaces, the space of symmetric positive-definite matrices, flag manifolds and Stiefel manifolds. The simulation is based on Wong--Zakai approximations of an appropriately chosen SDE in $G$ that is projected down onto $M\cong G/H$. The effectiveness lies in the fact that well-established results on the convergence rate of the Wong--Zakai equation immediately carry over to the homogeneous space thanks to Nash's embedding. The efficiency lies in the fact that explicit representations of the Wong--Zakai approximations can be obtained in this setting using the Lie exponential map.

title: GhostPrefix: Synchronization-Free Universal Prefix Attacks for ASR Manipulation
abstract: We present GhostPrefix, the first synchronization-free universal adversarial prefix attack against automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. Unlike prior audio attacks, which are typically crafted per utterance, require synchronization with the victim waveform, or target narrow objectives, GhostPrefix learns a short, reusable audio segment prepended to arbitrary live speech to exert real-time control over ASR outputs without knowledge of the future utterance or temporal alignment. A key challenge is maintaining stable adversarial effects across unknown, evolving speech contexts. GhostPrefix combines token-level losses with a novel representation-level objective for stable, input-agnostic effects. GhostPrefix supports three attack modes: (i) prompted prefix attacks for semantic steering, (ii) targeted prefix attacks for transcript hijacking, and (iii) untargeted prefix attacks for transcription degradation. To remain perceptually inconspicuous, we regularize prefixes toward benign environmental-sound distributions and improve robustness against over-the-air distortions. We evaluate GhostPrefix across 13 open-source ASR models from four families. In digital settings, it achieves average attack success rates of 97.6% for prompted steering and 93.4% for targeted hijacking, while driving word error rate to 1.18 under untargeted attacks. Over the air, it achieves success rates of 91.5% and 89.5% for prompted and targeted modes, respectively. These manipulations propagate into downstream AI-assisted pipelines, including voice assistants and AI note-taking tools, causing systematic semantic misinterpretations. GhostPrefix exposes synchronization-free universal prefixes as a practical, under-explored threat to real-world ASR and downstream applications. Artifacts and demos are available at https://ghostprefix.github.io/.

title: A Neural Network Approach towards Real-Time Knot Point Density Estimates for the Nonlinear Quadrotor
abstract: Spline representations provide a compact way to approximate continuous trajectories using a finite number of parameters. When approximating trajectories generated by dynamical systems, the efficiency of a spline representation depends strongly on the placement of knot points. Uniform knot distributions often lead to inefficient representations, requiring either unnecessary control points or producing poor approximations in regions where the trajectory varies rapidly. In this work we propose a learning-based method for adaptive knot placement in B-spline approximations of trajectories generated by ordinary differential equations. A neural network learns a mapping from the initial condition of the system to quantities that characterize the local variation of the resulting trajectory. These estimates are used to construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator, reducing the number of control points needed to meet a prescribed accuracy.

title: CausalXRL: Explainable Reinforcement Learning through Causal Graph Reasoning
abstract: Reinforcement learning is a powerful paradigm for training autonomous agents and has achieved impressive performance in complex environments. However, this success often comes at the cost of interpretability, diminishing trust and complicating efforts to debug and improve agent behavior. To address these challenges, we introduce CausalXRL, a novel framework for explainable reinforcement learning (XRL). A key feature of CausalXRL is its use of causal graph reasoning, which provides transparent, structured, multi-level explanations of agent decision-making. We validate CausalXRL through comprehensive case studies and a two-part evaluation: (1) a quantitative analysis of explanation fidelity and causal-structure learning efficiency in benchmark RL environments, and (2) a qualitative expert study assessing explainability in the real-time strategy (RTS) benchmark MicroRTS. The quantitative results show that CausalXRL can provide faithful explanations while efficiently learning causal structures, and the qualitative expert study suggests that participants found CausalXRL useful for inspecting high-level RTS strategies.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Classification: A Comparative Study with Classical Kernels
abstract: Quantum kernel methods are the most concrete near-term proposal for quantum machine learning on classical data, yet published benchmarks disagree on whether they outperform tuned classical kernels, and the disagreement cannot be resolved from the literature because the comparisons are not protocol-controlled. We argue that the obstacle is one of measurement, not theory: the usual setup fixes the quantum feature map's data scaling while grid-searching the classical kernel's hyperparameters, recomputes nothing per fold, and reports cost in simulator time. We therefore treat the comparison itself as the object of study and impose three controls. The bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical $γ$, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations. On top of these we run a factorial design of 324 cells in which dimensionality, training size, class separability and data structure are explicit covariates, together with four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation, and a cost sweep. The dominant effect we measure is not quantum: tuning the feature map's bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference we observe. Tuned quantum kernels are then statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The advantage on synthetic data is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map itself, and it shrinks with dimensionality (-0.0045 per qubit) while growing with sample size. Finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel needs $5\times10^{7}$ circuits at n = 10,000. Protocol variance is thus sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions.

title: There Is No Free Loop: When Does Looping a Trained Model Pay for Its Inference Compute?
abstract: Looping re-applies a block of layers so that each token passes through the block more than once. Adding a loop to a trained model is attractive because it leaves the parameter count, and hence the disk size, the memory footprint and the training cost unchanged. Unfortunately, every generated token pays for the loop. Re-applying m of N layers makes each token about (N+m)/N times as expensive. Loops that a model learns during large-scale pretraining justify this price, but whether loops added after pretraining justify this cost remains unclear. We compare a looped model with two simple baselines. We first compare it with the same model trained identically without the loop (equal parameters). Secondly, we compare it with the best unlooped use of the same inference floating-point operations (equal FLOPs). Across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B parameters, only the looped 0.8B model beats both baselines. At 4B and 9B, the looped model does not beat the first baseline, i.e. the same model trained without the loop. This is not because the benchmarks are too easy, since on the same benchmarks the unlooped 9B model still scores up to 13 points higher than the 4B model, showing that there is ample room for improvement. Introducing loops in an already pretrained model therefore only pays for small models with a fixed parameter budget.

title: Any Forcing: Any-Step Generality and One-Step Stability for Autoregressive Video Generation
abstract: Autoregressive video generation enables efficient inference through streaming prediction. However, existing methods are typically restricted to fixed sampling steps, limiting the flexibility to balance generation quality and efficiency, while one-step generation suffers from degraded visual quality and error accumulation over long sequences, leading to content drift and generation collapse. To address these issues, we propose Any Forcing, a unified framework for achieving Any-Step Generality and One-Step Stability. Specifically, we introduce a unified adversarial discriminator that jointly performs real-distribution alignment, inter-step consistency alignment, and first-frame quality enhancement, enabling flexible sampling while preserving one-step generation quality. Furthermore, we propose a training-free adaptive long-term memory selection mechanism that selects historical states based on global semantic relevance and local value contribution, while remapping their temporal positions to preserve temporal relationships within the memory cache, thereby enabling stable one-step long-video generation. Experiments demonstrate that Any Forcing achieves high-quality and stable one-step autoregressive video generation, achieving 20.9 FPS and 24.7 FPS for short and long video generation on a single H100 GPU, respectively.

title: Beyond Smart Homes: Characterizing IoT Vulnerabilities Across Sectors, Vendors, and Products
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has expanded beyond consumer smart homes to sectors, such as industrial systems, healthcare, and smart cities, broadening the IoT attack surface. Prior empirical work has focused on studying aggregate IoT vulnerability characteristics or specific protocols, so patching is directed by aggregate security guidance. However, if dominant weaknesses differ substantially across sectors or products, such uniform guidance misdirects the remediation effort. To address this gap, we present a fine-grained, data-driven analysis of IoT vulnerabilities using a dataset of more than 15,000 IoT specific CVEs. We design a pipeline to enrich noisy CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) metadata, normalizing vendors and products, then assigning product type and sector labels using lexical matching, fuzzy clustering, and LLM-assisted classification. We find meaningful differences in the weakness profile of IoT sectors. For example, healthcare is dominated by authentication and credential weaknesses, while automotive faces memory issues. More importantly, we find that weakness profiles are more similar across different product types from the same vendor than across the same product type built by different vendors. This suggests vendor-level factors such as shared code and development practices dominate weakness inheritance, making a vendor's disclosure history informative about its other products. Our findings suggest weakness classes should be used to prioritize remediation efforts.

title: Treedepth is NP-Hard on Planar Graphs of Maximum Degree 3
abstract: Treedepth is an important parameter in algorithmic graph theory. It is known that the problem of computing the treedepth of a graph is NP-hard. It has been an open problem whether treedepth can be computed in polynomial time when the input graph is restricted to be planar, or of bounded degree. Assuming $P \neq NP$, we answer both questions in the negative: Under polynomial-time Turing reductions, it is NP-hard to compute the treedepth of planar graphs with maximum degree 3. This degree bound is best possible, since treedepth can be computed efficiently on graphs of maximum degree 2.

title: A Momentum-weighted Interface Stabilization Approach for Fluid-Structure Interaction with Strong Added-Mass Effects
abstract: Partitioned fluid-structure interaction (FSI) schemes permit the reuse of optimized standalone solvers but can become unstable under strong fluid added-mass effects, particularly when structural inertia is small relative to fluid inertia. This work traces the instability to the discrepancy between the interface pressure Schur complements of the monolithic and Dirichlet- Neumann partitioned systems, as revealed by a fixed-point analysis of the linearized FSI problem. Motivated by this analysis, a momentum-weighted interface stabilization (MWIS) is proposed, in which the interface pressure block of the fluid subproblem is augmented by an operator constructed from the fluid and structural interface momentum operators. The augmentation is consistent by construction, vanishing at convergence so that the monolithic solution is recovered. A sparse diagonal approximation of the operator, derived from element metrics, limits intersolver data exchange to quantities comparable in size to standard interface coupling data while requiring minimal modifications to the standalone solvers. Numerical experiments, spanning a linear model and established nonlinear FSI benchmarks, demonstrate improved coupling robustness in regimes of strong added-mass where the standard Dirichlet-Neumann scheme diverges.

title: Distinguishing N$_2$-Dominated from O$_2$-Dominated Atmospheres on Terrestrial Exoplanets with Reflected-Light Spectroscopy
abstract: Reflected-light spectra of Earth-sized exoplanets promise to probe habitability and biosignatures, but interpreting atmospheric oxygen can be challenging because $O_2$ can arise from both biological and abiotic processes. In addition, reflected-light retrievals exhibit degeneracies among atmospheric composition, clouds, surface reflectance, and gravity. We use the Bayesian retrieval framework ExoReL$^\Re$, leveraging recent model developments that incorporate (i) $O_2$-$O_2$ collision-induced absorption (CIA), which produces the $O_4$ bands, and (ii) a wavelength-dependent (step-function) surface albedo parameterization. Focusing on a modern Earth analog, we compare retrievals with and without $O_2$-$O_2$ CIA using spectra within 0.25-1.8 $μ$m, and perform signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) sweeps for two observing configurations motivated by the Habitable Worlds Observatory: a resolved-visible case ($R_{VIS}=140$) and a broadband-visible case (three broad bins). Omitting $O_2$-$O_2$ CIA allows the retrieval to fit the spectrum with an incorrect $O_2$-dominated atmosphere. Including $O_2$-$O_2$ CIA leverages the $O_4$ bands to break this degeneracy and recover the correct $N_2$-dominated, $O_2$-rich solution without requiring a tight mass prior. Adopting a robustness criterion of $\ge95\%$ posterior mass in the $N_2$-dominated region, both configurations require SNR $\gtrsim20$ at 0.75 $μ$m (SNR $\approx14$ near the 1.27 $μ$m $O_4$ band for $R_{NIR}=70$) to identify the correct dominant gas, with higher cloud fraction increasing this threshold. Reducing near-IR coverage to 1.4 $μ$m prevents recovery of the correct $N_2$-dominated solution across the explored SNR range, and instead favors a spurious $O_2$-dominated, $CO_2$-rich atmosphere. These results support near-IR coverage to $\sim1.7$ $μ$m and SNR $\gtrsim20$ at 0.75 $μ$m for robust oxygen interpretation on Earth-like planets.

title: Learning Clean Generative Processes from Noisy Measurements
abstract: We study how to learn a generative model of clean images using only noisy observations. Diffusion processes and their generalizations to non-Gaussian noise require posterior predictions at every noise level. We first show that it is possible to learn these predictions from independent noisy views using Noise2Noise regression, but only at or above the noise level of the training data. To learn the predictions below that level, needed to generate clean images, we impose consistency: a prediction should equal its expectation after continuing the sampling process. We derive conditions under which consistency uniquely determines the continuation to the clean image distribution and verify them for Poisson, binomial, Gamma, and negative-binomial measurements. Experiments on CIFAR-10, photon-counting microscopy, and synthetic aperture radar show that the required posterior predictions can be learned from noisy views alone and that the consistency relation repairs the continuation beyond the noise level of the data, which severely deteriorates without consistency.

title: Meson spectroscopy from lattice QCD
abstract: Determining the meson spectrum directly from Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) remains a central challenge, since QCD is strongly coupled at low energies and most excited states appear as resonances in hadronic decay channels. Advances in lattice QCD and scattering theory now provide a systematic framework for extracting meson spectra and resonance properties from first principles. Here I present an overview of this program and review current state-of-the-art calculations in meson spectroscopy from lattice QCD. I highlight recent progress in the extraction of resonant and coupled-channel amplitudes, along with frontier developments in three-body dynamics and the determination of meson photo-couplings. Together, these advances are bringing us closer to a comprehensive first-principles description of the excited meson spectrum.

title: Berenstein-Zelevinsky polytopes for type $\mathrm{G}_{2}$
abstract: In 2001, Berenstein and Zelevinsky presented a polyhedral model for the problem of computing tensor-product multiplicities for semi\-simple Lie algebras. We provide explicit linear equations and inequalities for Berenstein--Zelevinsky (BZ) polytopes of type-$\mathrm{G}_{2}$ Lie algebras. We prove that the denominator of a type-$\mathrm{G}_{2}$ BZ~polytope divides $180$, and that this bound is sharp, while the quasi-period of the Ehrhart quasipolynomial of such a polytope is always a divisor of $6$. We also show that BZ~polytopes of type-$\mathrm{G}_{2}$ Lie algebras can fail to satisfy Ehrhart positivity, in contrast to a conjectured property of BZ~polytopes for all classical types.

title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
abstract: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice?
